6. open questions worth having an opinion on

can NIXL get BLHNC’s one-descriptor-per-block win back without re-breaking hetero TP? the obvious move: whole-row registration under homogeneous TP, per-layer strided regions under hetero TP, chosen per remote engine at handshake. the cost: two registrations of the same memory, or descriptors built per (remote engine, tp_ratio). the split-handle cache keyed by (tp_ratio, remote_block_size) already exists (base_worker.py:790).
for Qwen4Exp the same split would lift the TP1↔TP≥2 ban: you’d keep whole-row descriptors on the replicated side and emit per-member, head-offset descriptors when one side still holds 2 heads per page.
is BHLNC worth unblocking for dense models? it needs a NIXL descriptor model at (block, head-range) granularity instead of (region, block), kernels with arbitrary head stride, and it stays illegal under HMA. dense-only means not DSV4, not Kimi K3, not qwen4-next.
does the RFC’s jointly_contiguous_chunks subsume all of this? if P and D each describe their physical layout as a meta tensor, the connector can compute maximal runs contiguous in both layouts and emit exactly those descriptors. then the layout choice becomes a pure perf knob instead of a correctness constraint, and P and D could even run different layouts. that’s the end state the RFC is pointing at.
should P and D be allowed to disagree on layout? today only one asymmetric pair works (LBHNC→LBNHC with permute). with (3), any pair could work at the cost of more, smaller descriptors.


project knowledge note: the knowledge/ files in this project predate all of this (they still call FlashAttentionBackend.get_kv_cache_shape, which [1/N] removed). don’t read layout semantics off them.

0. One-screen summary

What it is: a Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 hybrid (GDN + gated attention, 512-expert MoE, MTP, Qwen3-VL vision tower). It adds four new pieces:

QSA = Qwen Sparse Attention. Every full-attention layer becomes block-sparse GQA. A small weight-free indexer picks the 512 most relevant 4-token blocks, i.e. a 2048-token budget.
HC = Hyper-Connections, “Gated Residual” variant. The residual stream has 4 branches of width H. There is no branch-to-branch mixing matrix.
PLE = an n-gram hash embedding. It is named after Gemma-3n Per-Layer Embedding, but the math is DeepSeek Engram’s. It sits in 1 layer and uses a 51B-parameter table kept in pinned host memory and read over UVA.
MTP: a QSA layer that is HC-aware and can reuse the indexer’s top-k across draft steps.


Derived shapes [derived from nvidia/low_latency_gemm.py:27-290 plan keys + config defaults; verify against the HF config.json, which I could not fetch]:

hidden H = 2560. HC streams = 4, so the residual is 10240 wide. hc_lowrank = 320.
QSA: 24 Q heads, 2 KV heads, head_dim 256. Rotary dim is 64 (partial factor 0.25).
Indexer: 4 heads × 128, 1 KV head.
GDN: 16 QK heads and 48 V heads, head_dim 128.
MoE: 512 routed experts, 1 shared expert with intermediate size 640. Padded vocab is 248,320.
Third-party card: 48 layers = 36 GDN + 12 QSA, top-10 routing [web, unverified].

Size: 125B MoE + 51B n-gram table, about 6B active [web]. Sources disagree on whether the 51B is included in or added to the 125B.

Layer types come from config.layer_types. Two values exist:

"linear_attention" builds GDN (QwenGatedDeltaNetAttention, gqa_interleaved_layout=False, the Qwen3.5 flat qkvz layout) (model.py:209-215).
"qwen_sparse_attention", renamed "indexed_attention" in Transformers 5.18 (model.py:82-84). This builds QSA when indexer_n_heads is set, and plain Qwen3NextAttention otherwise (model.py:216-233).

GDN still dominates, at a 3:1 ratio (“one full-attention layer every four”) [web: arXiv 2608.30320, Swift docs]. The code takes the ratio from layer_types and does not hard-code it.

Routed expert count 512 comes from the router GEMM shape (512, 2560) (low_latency_gemm.py:198).
Shared expert: gate is (1,2560), gate_up is (1280,2560), so the intermediate size is 640 (low_latency_gemm.py:173-222).
Top-k = 10 [web, unverified].



1.4 MTP — nvidia/mtp.py

Layer. One MTP layer, built as Qwen4ExpDecoderLayer(layer_type="qwen_sparse_attention"). It is a full QSA layer with its own indexer and caches, plus HC and MoE (mtp.py:210-216). PLE is forced off because input_ids is None (mtp.py:316-324).
Input fusion (“residual_linear_shared”).

fc_embedding(norm(emb)) gives [T,H].
fc_hidden is shared across the 4 streams and applied to norm(h_multi) [T,4,H].
The embedding enters as prev_block_output with unit injection, so it is added to every stream (mtp.py:146-168, 295-308). #54687 reuses the HC combine-norm kernel here.

Target hidden is multi-stream (“scheme A”). The target model keeps the pre-final-mixer [T,4H] in _mtp_hidden_buffer (max_num_batched_tokens × 10240 × 2 B ≈ 160 MiB at 8192 tokens) (model.py:424-442, 563-568). The drafter returns (sample [T,H], multi [T,4H]) and feeds multi to the next step (mtp.py:330-340).
index_share_for_mtp_iteration.

Step 0 runs the top-k.
Steps ≥ 1 set indexer.skip_topk=True. They still update the side caches but reuse step-0 rows, which are compacted to target-aligned rows via compact_topk_indices (mtp.py:248-269; indexer_qsa.py:128-130, 409-412).

Takeaway: vLLM is converging on a small set of generic primitives: per-request ring scratch (CircularBufferSpec), fractional-token compressed rows (tokens_per_state), TP-replicated Mamba-like state (tp_replicated), host-resident hashed tables (EngramConfig), B-outer packed pages, and breakable graphs. Qwen4Exp and DSV4.1 are the two main consumers. A fix to one (for example #59528) usually touches both.

Cache invariants and the layout planner

Ring sizing.

It must hold the committed members of the open group plus every draft row written before acceptance. Too small, and a rejected draft overwrites a committed key that the next step still needs to close the group (qsa_cache.py:845-851; tests test_qsa_circular_buffer_survives_one_speculative_step).
Its capacity must divide the attention block_size, because it joins the LCM that sets the scheduler block size (qsa_cache.py:852-855).
Examples: num_spec=1 gives 8 slots; num_spec=5 gives 12 slots, which forces block_size to be a multiple of 12 [derived].


Ring slot mapping: slot = block_table[req,0]·cap + pos % cap. Only the last cap rows of each request’s chunk are written (token_idx + cap >= query_end). Requests on the null block (block 0) are skipped (qsa_cache.py:108-158, 281-297; #59528).
Compressed slot mapping: written only at group-closing positions (pos+1)%c==0. It is masked by the main slot_mapping < 0 (qsa_cache.py:161-189, 298-320).
Packing.

Ring slot mapping: slot = block_table[req,0]·cap + pos % cap. Only the last cap rows of each request’s chunk are written (token_idx + cap >= query_end). Requests on the null block (block 0) are skipped (qsa_cache.py:108-158, 281-297; #59528).
Compressed slot mapping: written only at group-closing positions (pos+1)%c==0. It is masked by the main slot_mapping < 0 (qsa_cache.py:161-189, 298-320).
Packing.

QSAStateBackend.supported_kv_cache_layouts = (BLNHC, BLHNC). The reason given: “QSA pages are packed beside the main KV pages within each block” (qsa_cache.py:753-756).
Mixed page sizes force a block-compact layout, and with more than one group, a block-outermost one (validate_kv_cache_layout, v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:1555-1585, _get_packed_kv_cache_groups :1860+).
This is the BLHNC-vs-LBHNC layout RFC #42082 (v1/kv_cache_layout.py:11-28) in practice. Qwen4Exp requires B-outer layouts.


Mamba page size. Two Mamba specs (GDN, PLE) are present, and the platform takes the max page size (vllm/platforms/interface.py:1044-1050).

The PLE page is TP-replicated while GDN shrinks with TP.
[derived] At TP=8 with bf16 SSM: GDN ≈ 192 KiB + 15 KiB versus PLE 200–240 KiB. So PLE becomes the largest page at high TP or high num_spec.

Prefix caching

CircularBufferManager claims exactly 1 block per request. It reports a cache hit of 0, and its cache and skip hooks do nothing (v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1206-1295).
The coordinator excludes non-cacheable groups from hit lookup and from block-size divisibility (v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:670-679, 730-740).
Why this is correct [infer]: hits are aligned to block_size, which is a multiple of the ring capacity and so of c. At a hit boundary the open group is empty, so the compressor never needs ring rows from before the hit.
GDN state needs mamba-cache-mode align or checkpoints. The ROCm eval config uses --mamba-cache-mode align (tests/evals/qwen4_exp/configs/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8-rocm.yaml).
MooncakeStore (prefix-store semantics) excludes the ring group (#55027).

P/D (NIXL) — the “CSA-linear” path in distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py:

Detection. CSA-linear is detected when any group is a CircularBufferSpec (:577-598). It allows at most one TP-replicated MambaSpec group (the PLE) with exactly one layer.
What transfers.

The ring IS transferred (the scratch-region descriptors, :237-243). Unlike a prefix hit, the end of a P/D prompt is arbitrary, so the decode side needs the open group’s raw keys.
The whole PLE conv page is copied from one source rank, with descriptors sized by _ple_block_len and not by the region’s block_len (#59997, :1912-1926, :1982).

The ring IS transferred (the scratch-region descriptors, :237-243). Unlike a prefix hit, the end of a P/D prompt is arbitrary, so the decode side needs the open group’s raw keys.
The whole PLE conv page is copied from one source rank, with descriptors sized by _ple_block_len and not by the region’s block_len (#59997, :1912-1926, :1982).


Heterogeneous TP constraint (relevant to your hetero-TP work). _validate_csa_linear_tp_layout (:967-989) rejects pairs that sit on opposite sides of the KV-head sharding boundary.

With 2 KV heads: P TP1 (2 heads per page) ↔ D TP≥2 (1 head per page, replicated) is rejected.
P TP2 ↔ D TP4 is fine.
Cause: the main KV and QSA side pages are packed in one block and move as whole block units.


NIXL host staging is not supported with CSA-linear (:1397-1400). The decode side also needs the conv layout VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS (:600-612).
supports_kv_connector() = False on Qwen4ExpQSAFlashAttentionBackend (qsa.py:204-206). That flag only matters in backend selection (v1/attention/backend.py:339), and the QSA owner hard-wires its backend (qsa.py:472). [infer: it is effectively inert; P/D is exercised through the CSA-linear tests above.]
PLE on the decode side needs only ngram_context (the last 2 tokens), and model_state rebuilds it from the token history. Contrast DSV4.1 Engram, whose hash_cache slots don’t travel with KV and so needs lookback_token_ids (vllm/models/deepseek_v41/common/engram.py:3-35).

CUDA graphs / DP / offload

CUDA graphs.

NVIDIA uses breakable CUDA graphs with no torch.compile (#55272).
Eager breaks sit at _run_qsa (qsa.py:553), _short_conv (ple_layer.py:334), start_prefetch and _finalize_prefetch.
QSA and the side-cache metadata builders are UNIFORM_BATCH (qsa.py:140-143, qsa_cache.py:599-602), so spec verify is treated as uniform decode.


Pinned prefetch.

CUDA graphs / DP / offload

CUDA graphs.

NVIDIA uses breakable CUDA graphs with no torch.compile (#55272).
Eager breaks sit at _run_qsa (qsa.py:553), _short_conv (ple_layer.py:334), start_prefetch and _finalize_prefetch.
QSA and the side-cache metadata builders are UNIFORM_BATCH (qsa.py:140-143, qsa_cache.py:599-602), so spec verify is treated as uniform decode.


Pinned prefetch.

The buffer is allocated lazily but must exist before capture; capture raises otherwise (common/ngram_embedding.py:530-554).
The ids live in a persistent _prefetch_ids buffer because the side-stream lookup outlives the eager-break args, whose graph-pool memory a later segment can reuse (#58489, ngram_embedding.py:225-230).


DP.

With embedding_across_dp, every DP rank must run the PLE all_gather each step, including dummy batches, and needs dp_metadata (common/ngram_embedding.py:112-127).
dp_shared_memory is the default when DP > 1 and elastic EP is off.


Profiling. The ring and compressed views must not hold extra storage refs, or the profiling KV cannot be freed (#58961, qsa_cache.py:831-842).

5. Sharp edges (bugs that expose invariants)

The ring must never touch the null block (#59528).

Dummy and padding requests sit on block 0. The ring formula blk·cap + pos%cap would scribble on the shared null page.
Guard: valid &= physical_block > 0 (qsa_cache.py:130-132, 293-294). Every other spec type uses >= 0.
Invariant: per-request scratch (one block per request) may not alias the null block.


Ring capacity under spec decode (qsa_cache.py:845-855).

Draft rows are written before acceptance. Capacity is rounded up to a multiple of c and must divide block_size. Otherwise a rejected draft overwrites committed keys of the open group.
DSV4.1’s compressor sizes its ring as max(8, pow2 ≥ num_spec+2) instead (models/deepseek_v41/compressor.py:150-153).

1. The idea
What is cached
Baseline Mamba2 decode (selective_state_update) does a read-modify-write of the full state S ∈ R^{nheads×headdim×dstate} every token.
ReplaySSM keeps:

a checkpoint S_0: the same ssm_state slot, now written only on a flush.
a small ring of recent per-token inputs per request slot: x_cache (nheads, L, headdim) in the activation dtype, dt_cache (nheads, L) in fp32 (post-softplus, post-bias), B_cache (ngroups, L, dstate) in the activation dtype. Shapes: mamba_utils.py:223-254. Dtypes: mamba_utils.py:86-95.
C is not cached. It is the current token’s query.

Why replay is exact (up to fp)
Mamba2 with scalar-per-head A (TIE*HDIM, asserted at selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only.py:547-554):
S_t = a_t S*{t-1} + Δ*t x_t B_tᵀ, y_t = S_t C_t + D x_t, with a_t = exp(A Δ_t).

Why replay is exact (up to fp)
Mamba2 with scalar-per-head A (TIE*HDIM, asserted at selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only.py:547-554):
S_t = a_t S*{t-1} + Δ*t x_t B_tᵀ, y_t = S_t C_t + D x_t, with a_t = exp(A Δ_t).
Unroll hsteps from the checkpoint. Letpre_j = Σ*{i≤j} Δ_i:

S_t = e^{A·pre_t} S_0 + Σ_{j≤t} Δ_j e^{A(pre_t − pre_j)} x_j B_jᵀ (state route, used on flush)
y_t = e^{A·pre_t} (S_0 C_t) + Σ_j s_{j,t} x_j (B_jᵀ C_t) (output-only route, which never materializes S_t)

This is the linear-attention identity: a decayed “KV” sum plus a checkpoint readout. Kernel comment at selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only.py:280-282. B_jᵀC_t depends only on the group, so it is precomputed once per (row, group) by _replayssm_output_only_precompute_kernel (:25-118) into the fp32 bc_pre scratch. That is a 16× reuse for 128 heads / 8 groups.
“Output only” and “standard decode”

standard decode means plain autoregressive decode with 1 token per request per step, no spec. PR #48018 was standard-decode only (config rejected num_speculative_tokens > 0; see the #48018 diff of vllm/config/vllm.py).
output-only kernel (_replayssm_output_only_kernel, :135-478) has two branches, selected per row by is_flush:

non-flush (:279-361): read S_0 (yes, still read every step), dt/x history, and bc_pre. Compute y by the output-only formula. Append (x, dt, B) at write_pos. No state store.
flush (:362-462): rebuild S_t = decay·S_0 + X·(scale⊙B) with one tl.dot per dstate tile. Store it as the new checkpoint, then y = S_t C. The current token is folded in and not appended.

Triton cursor: write_pos = (num_computed − decode_base) mod L, flush iff write_pos == L−1 (mamba_attn.py:554-572). So L tokens fold per flush, physical row L−1 is never written, and L=1 degenerates to “flush every step”, which is the baseline plus overhead.

With bf16 state: 4 MiB vs ≈2.29 MiB, so 0.57× (≤1.75×). The blog gives the same structure per head: baseline 8dn + 2(d+2n+1), ReplaySSM 4dn + 2h(d+n+1) + … with fp32 state. Only the write is amortized.
Memory overhead of the ring: 256 + 8 + 32 = 296 KiB per slot per layer, which is 7.2% of a 4 MiB fp32 state and 14.5% of a bf16 state (Nano-4B, 96×80×128: 278 KiB = 7.2%). The ring lives inside the same Mamba page (MambaSpec.shapes has 5 tensors; abstract.py:66-84), so it is charged against KV blocks.
When it wins / loses
Wins: large-batch decode where the SSU is HBM-bound (state ≫ per-token inputs). Bigger dstate·headdim per head means a bigger win. Spec decode wins more (§3): baseline writes T states per verify, while replay writes ~0.
Loses or neutral:

L=1 (pure overhead). Very large L: the per-step history read grows ∝ L·(d+n). The blog shows a bell curve, with best L = 8 for Nemotron-3 and 16 for Qwen3.5. vLLM’s default is 16 (config/cache.py:203), and the kernel test comment calls 8 “the production buffer length” (test_replayssm_standard_decode_mamba2.py:330). These two disagree.
small batch / latency-bound: 2 kernel launches (precompute always launches, :602-604), plus a CPU write_pos derivation and H2D copy per step (Triton).
align-mode prefix caching forces extra flushes at every mamba block boundary (mamba_attn.py:574-580).
7–15% more Mamba memory per slot in standard decode (but far less memory under MTP, §3).
end-to-end gain is diluted by MoE/attention time (blog: 1.84× kernel becomes ≤1.48× e2e).


3. MTP / spec decode (#52928)
FlashInfer only. The model runs T = 1+K tokens per request off one checkpoint:

Delayed commit. The acceptance count for query N is only known at query N+1. The first ReplaySSM layer of the group runs commit_replayssm_ring_trackers before conv/SSU (mamba_mixer2.py:908-935 → ssu_dispatch.py:77-130):

must_ckpt = prev_query_len>0 && prev + prev_query_len > L (this mirrors the decision the kernel made last step).
if must_ckpt: ring_start += prev (mod ring_len), prev = accepted. Otherwise prev += accepted. Then set prev_query_len = current T.

if must_ckpt: ring_start += prev (mod ring_len), prev = accepted. Otherwise prev += accepted. Then set prev_query_len = current T.


Verify. checkpointing_ssu(state, rings, ring_start, prev, x[b,T], …) replays prev committed rows, appends T rows, and computes T causal outputs. FlashInfer docs give the flush rule as pnat + 2T > RING_BUFFER_LEN (equivalently prev + T > L, since ring = L+T) and “the HOST owns bookkeeping: advance by the replayed count on flush”. update_trackers=False under spec (mixer2:1039).
Rejection = do nothing. Rejected rows sit past the committed prefix and are overwritten by the next append. No per-draft state was ever written, so there is nothing to roll back. Conv state still uses num_accepted_tokens in causal_conv1d_update. max_query_len is forced to 1+K because the state block table now has one column (mixer2:944-952).
Layout: if the batch is uniform (num_decode_tokens == B·T), view as (B, T, H, D) and drop cu_seqlens. Otherwise use the varlen path with cu_seqlens/max_seqlen (mixer2:990-1017). Prefill rows reclassified as decode get num_accepted = diff(query_start_loc) (mamba_attn.py:490-499).

Compared with per-token states (baseline spec): the baseline allocates 1+K state slots per request and writes T states per verify (num_speculative_blocks=K). For K=3 with the geometry above: baseline is 4 × 4 MiB = 16 MiB per req-layer, replay is 4 MiB + 370 KiB ring = 4.36 MiB → 3.67× less. The blog measured 3.0–3.3× more max concurrency, 2.28–3.33× kernel, and ≤2.14× over the baseline spec path. The extra complexity is the delayed commit, cursor sharing across layers, a GPU-side commit kernel (no host sync), and the incompatibility with align mode and P/D.
Ring trace (tests/kernels/mamba/test_ssu_dispatch.py:96-175, L=16, K=3, ring=20, all accepted): (start,prev,qlen): (0,0,4)→(0,4,4)…(0,16,4)→(16,4,4)…(16,16,4)→(12,4,4). Each checkpoint moves start by 16 mod 20.

Test models are Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-BF16 (Triton) and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 (FlashInfer; FI 0.7.0 can’t compile Nano’s headdim=80), per tests/v1/e2e/test_replayssm_decode.py:14-16.

It is spec-decode only (kda.py:594-596) and caches per-window correction (H,T,dv) fp32 and k‖g (H,T,2dk) (mamba_utils.py:330-347), not x,B,dt. The delta rule’s correction β(v − S k) depends on the state, so you cache the correction, and then recovery is linear rank-1 folding. This is the same move the blog uses for GDN. ROCm is excluded (test_registry.py:157-158).
Qwen4Exp (GDN, vllm/models/qwen4_exp/*/model.py → QwenGatedDeltaNetAttention): no replay upstream. GDN ReplaySSM exists only in the research fork (fused_recurrent_replayssm.py, gdn_replayssm_spec_decode.py, per its README).
Unrelated “replay” terms:

DSv4.1 decoder replay layers (vllm/models/deepseek_v41/decoder_replay_layers.py:1-13; #58132, #59532, #59894). After the last KV-source layer, the later SWA-only layers run on each request’s trailing window rows as a sub-batch.
SWA bounded replay (config/cache.py:250-255, #56227 encoder-side, #58132 decoder-side, #59197 skip when the KV load carries the window). SWA KV is kept out of prefix caching and rebuilt after a hit by recomputing the last window.
CUDA graph replay: re-launching captured graphs. It is why ReplaySSM uses persistent buffers and always launches both kernels.
Mooncake EAGLE replay boundary (#54713, #61012; v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:65-86 replay_boundaries). These are prefix positions a resend or extension can resume at (EAGLE drops back one block), so SWA tails and Mamba checkpoints are retained there.
Also unrelated: routing replay (R3), mask replay, trace replay in vllm bench.




6. Sharp edges

Why near-ties flip. Replay changes the arithmetic, not the math. Decay is computed as one exp(A·Σdt), not a product of per-step exp(AΔ). Output-only and flush steps use different routes. The flush route rounds scale⊙B to the activation dtype before the GEMM (:419-421), which the tests model as “bf16 reconstruction”. With bf16 state, the baseline rounds the state every step, while replay rounds once per flush (more accurate, still different), so the tests do not even compare against the baseline at bf16 state (test_replayssm_standard_decode_mamba2.py:16-19). Greedy argmax flips at near-ties, so the e2e tests compare top-5 logprobs, not ids (test_replayssm_decode.py:56-58).
#60515 specifically: the NVFP4 FlashInfer model “is not reproducible across engine instances”. Baseline and replay run in separate engines, so near-tie prompts failed for reasons unrelated to replay. The new prompts avoid near-ties and decode >16 tokens so at least one flush/checkpoint is exercised (test_replayssm_decode.py:28-33). This is test hygiene, not a kernel fix.
fp32 parity needs tf32x3. Plain TF32 in the flush tl.dot drifts by about 1e-2 with fp32 activations, versus 1e-5 for a correct reconstruction. The test atol of 1e-3 is placed to catch that (test_replayssm_standard_decode_mamba2.py:47-54). ROCm Triton lacks tf32x3, so it uses the backend default (selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only.py:584-586). That only matters for fp32 activations, since bf16/fp16 inputs are cast first. I did not verify what the ROCm default precision is.

Prefill/decode equivalence (tests/kernels/mamba/test_replayssm_prefill_decode_equivalence_mamba2.py:3-25): SSD chunked prefill is about 2e-2 (fp32) / 4–6e-2 (bf16) from the exact recurrence, while replay decode is about 2e-6. All paths are anchored to the fp32 recurrence at SSD-level tolerances. The production dt flow (softplus + per-head bias ≈ −4) keeps decays well-conditioned. dt_cache is fp32 so recomputed decays don’t amplify bf16 dt error through exp.
Stochastic rounding (fp16 state, Blackwell cvt.rs) runs only on flush, at 1/L of the baseline rate (:435-455).
State/cursor coupling. The checkpoint is stale between flushes, so anything that copies ssm_state alone gets a wrong state: KV offload, P/D, prefix caching in non-align mode. Hence the KV-connector ban and align-mode forced boundary flushes. FlashInfer cursors live outside the page and are reset on every prefill (mixer2:897-904).
Triton requires exact CPU sequence lengths: it is incompatible with async spec decode (mamba_attn.py:526-535) and with MRV2.

grill questions (answer key follows each)
Q1. During a 10k-token prefill, layers 21..39 compute only 128 rows per request, yet decode later attends over all 10k positions at those layers. Where does that global KV come from, and what exactly is lost?

Ratio-1 layers 21..39 own no compressed cache. They read layer 20’s full-length (ratio-1) cache plus index K, both projected from layer 20’s input H(L/2). write_kv writes these for every row before trimming (nvidia/model.py:627-659, attention.py:689-715, get_kv_cache_spec returns None for non-sources :1143). What is lost is exactness of the decoder layers’ SWA KV and hidden states for the first rows of the window: their SWA is clamped at kv_start = max(replay_start, seq_len−128) (model_state.py:131-134). That is the report’s train-aware approximation.

Q2. Why did #59894 move the replay cut from layer 21 to layer 20, and what state did that let it delete?

Layers 21..23 consume topk_indices_buffer, and 24..36 consume candidate_block_buffer, both written per row by layer 20’s indexer (index and candidate source). With the cut at 21, those row-indexed buffers held full-batch rows and had to be compacted in place to replay rows (row_buffers, removed in the diff). With layer 20 inside the replay batch, its indexer writes per-replay-row directly. The KV that every row needs is produced by forward_kv beforehand, which is also why layer 20’s SWA metadata keeps the batch’s replay_start rather than kept_kv_start (model_state.py:529-542).

Q3. Derive 890 B/token, and say what changes on H200.

Q3. Derive 890 B/token, and say what changes on H200.

SM100 + mega attention + nvfp4_ds_mla + MXFP4 indexer: main = 288·(½+½+½+1) = 720, index = 68·(½+½+½+1) = 170. On H200 (SM90) _use_v41_mxfp8_kv_record() is False, so the record is the 584 B V4 record (576-aligned) and NVFP4 is rejected (attention.py:128-130, 523-527): 584·2.5 = 1460 + index (132·2.5 = 330 FP8) ≈ 1790.

Q4. A request hits 1000 cached tokens through local prefix caching, with block size 256 and window 128. Walk through the scheduler and worker.

The hit is 768, because local hits are block-aligned; external hits are trimmed by ext_tokens -= ext_tokens % block_size, scheduler.py:1004. 768 > 128, so it is kept. _mark_prefix_replay sets replay_start = 640 and rewinds num_computed_tokens to 640 (:3113-3131). The worker pads slots for positions 640..767 in all prefix-cacheable groups, so compressed, index-K and ring writes are skipped (model_state.py:69-98, compressor_utils.py:197-203). Only SWA KV is rebuilt, with SWA clamped at 640 (sparse_swa.py:369-371). Tokens 768+ compute normally.

Q5. Same request, but the KV arrives through NIXL P/D. What differs, and why does P stop at N−1?

NIXL reports all transfer groups loaded (nixl/connector.py:170-171), SWA included, so _load_restores_replay_window is True: no block trim, replay_start=0 (scheduler.py:993-1004, 3104-3111). P computes N−1 tokens (_prefill_backoff, nixl/base_scheduler.py:379-395) so the transferred window is laid out for the last token D recomputes; replay would not fix it after a load. A Mooncake store / CPU offload hit returns only the prefix-cacheable groups and replays.

Q6. Engram at layer 14 needs the token ids at p−1..p−3. Where do they come from on a P/D decode instance’s first chunk, and why not from the KV cache?

The slot hash_cache is keyed on the first local layer’s SWA slots, but it is not KV, so a transfer does not fill it. MRv2 passes lookback_token_ids gathered from req_states.all_token_ids at num_computed−1−k (model_state.py:41-66, 278-298), and they take precedence (engram.py:27-35). Without them, the model raises unless the slot cache is in use (nvidia/model.py:956-965).

Q7. You port V4’s build_deepseek_v4_rope unchanged. Which layers break, and how?

V4 selects compress_rope_theta and YaRN iff compress_ratio > 1. In V4.1, ratio 1 is a compressed layer, so layers 20..39 (and layer 20’s compressor insert) would get theta 10000 with no YaRN. Their compressed KV and queries would be rotated inconsistently with the checkpoint (M41/common/rope.py:23-33).

Q8. Why is the ratio-2 compressor ring safe to exclude from prefix caching, and what was #58560?

V4 selects compress_rope_theta and YaRN iff compress_ratio > 1. In V4.1, ratio 1 is a compressed layer, so layers 20..39 (and layer 20’s compressor insert) would get theta 10000 with no YaRN. Their compressed KV and queries would be rotated inconsistently with the checkpoint (M41/common/rope.py:23-33).

Q8. Why is the ratio-2 compressor ring safe to exclude from prefix caching, and what was #58560?

Prefix hits must align to every cacheable spec’s tokens_per_state (kv_cache_utils.py:887-897). Ratio 2 forces even hits, so no open group spans a hit boundary, and the ring only ever holds the current open group plus spec drafts (capacity ≥ k+2, compressor.py:150-153). #58560: padding and dummy rows map to block 0 (null), and the ring kernel wrote 0*cap+pos%cap into it. Fix: mask block != 0 (compressor.py:78-84).

Q9. In layer l, which pre-mix collapses the attention input and which the FFN input? What collapses the final output, and why must Engram finalize the preceding MoE?

Attention uses the pre-mix carried in from layer l−1’s FFN (identity / copy 0 for layer 0). The FFN uses layer l’s attention pre-mix (model.py:491-493, 599-613). The final collapse uses the last FFN pre-mix, since there is no hc_head (:1066-1070). Engram needs the explicit previous post (mhc_post_tilelang) on the full hc stream before its own pre (:531-561). That stops the post from folding into the fused post+pre GEMM, so the layer before it cannot defer its MoE finalize into that boundary’s all-reduce (:789-798).

Q10. You enable a custom drafter with sliding_window 256 on V4.1. What silently changes, and why?

Q10. You enable a custom drafter with sliding_window 256 on V4.1. What silently changes, and why?

Decoder replay is disabled (_decoder_replay_supported, model.py:1227-1235). The drafter reads target aux hidden states at layers 37..39, which exist only for the last 128 kept rows in replay steps. A wider-window or non-SWA drafter would read zeros (trimmed rows stay zero, decoder_replay_layers.py:125-130). Prefill then pays for all 40 layers on every token. DSpark itself is fine: window 128, all sliding_attention, context KV only for the window.

Kimi K3
Grill questions (answer key)
Q1. Kimi K3 is a hybrid model. Why does its MLAAttentionSpec set max_tp_shards=1, while the KDA MambaSpec is TP-sharded? What does this imply for per-GPU memory at TP8 and 1M context?
A. The MLA cache is one latent “head”, num_kv_heads=1, head_size=576 (mla.py:417-433). It is identical on every TP rank, so it is replicated. KDA state has shape (96/TP,128,128) (mamba_utils.py:326). Per GPU per sequence: MLA ≈ 27.6 GB (bf16, 24 layers × 1152 B × 1M) vs KDA ≈ 56 MB. Long context needs DCP to shard the MLA tokens. TP does not help MLA.
Q2. Write the K3 KDA gate. What breaks if gate_lower_bound is missing?
A. g = lb·σ(exp(A_log)·(raw+dt_bias)), with lb ∈ [-5,0) (recoverssm.py:17-33, kda.py:609-615). Without it, FlashKDA, the FlashInfer prefill, and FlashInfer spec are all unsupported (kda.py:240,356,377). The prefill falls back to Triton, kda_prefill_checkpoint_alignment returns None, and num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks=0, so internal prefill checkpoints are disabled (kda_checkpoint.py:16-17, kda.py:829-837).
Q3. In AttnRes, what are the “keys”, “query” and “values”? Is the query token-dependent?
A. Keys are the RMS-normalized sources (completed block sums plus the current partial sum) dotted with norm_w ⊙ w. The query w is a static per-layer vector (*_res_proj, 7168→1). Values are the un-normalized sources. Only the keys depend on the token (attn_res.py:102-146). The mixed vector is then RMS-normed with input_layernorm.weight and fed to attention.
Q4. How many AttnRes sources does the final LM-head mix see, and what does blocks[0] hold?

A. Keys are the RMS-normalized sources (completed block sums plus the current partial sum) dotted with norm_w ⊙ w. The query w is a static per-layer vector (*_res_proj, 7168→1). Values are the un-normalized sources. Only the keys depend on the token (attn_res.py:102-146). The mixed vector is then RMS-normed with input_layernorm.weight and fed to attention.
Q4. How many AttnRes sources does the final LM-head mix see, and what does blocks[0] hold?
A. num_attn_res_blocks = cdiv(93,12) = 8 (model.py:1171-1175), plus the partial prefix (layers 84–92), for 9 sources. blocks[0] = token embedding, written at layer 0 with block_write_idx=0 (model.py:975-977,1024-1035). The native kernel’s num_blocks ≤ 8 limit matches exactly (attn_res.py:196).
Q5. Native vs RecoverSSM spec decode for KDA: what is stored per draft token, and how is the post-acceptance state produced?
A. Native stores a full state per draft position (spec_state_indices[:, :k+1], num_speculative_blocks=k), and the next step indexes the accepted slot via num_accepted_tokens (kda.py:1136-1150). RecoverSSM stores c_t (fp32, [H,1+k,128]) and [k̂|raw_g] (bf16, [H,1+k,256]). It never writes S during verify. Commit replays S←exp(g)S + c kᵀ for the accepted prefix across all layers in one kernel (recoverssm.py:63-231,399-585,909). Memory per layer for k=7: about 44 MB vs 0.79 MB.
Q6. Why does FlashKDAPrefillCheckpointExporter read raw QKV rows to build the checkpoint conv state rather than the conv output?

Q6. Why does FlashKDAPrefillCheckpointExporter read raw QKV rows to build the checkpoint conv state rather than the conv output?
A. The conv state is the last W-1=3 inputs to the causal conv, so the exporter copies raw_qkv[ckpt_end-3 : ckpt_end] (kda_checkpoint.py:101-119). The recurrent part comes from FlashKDA’s checkpoint_state at checkpoint_offsets (kda.py:1211-1245). Both land in the block reserved at cdiv(num_tokens,B)-2.
Q7. State the conditions under which a prefill chunk may export an internal checkpoint.
A. All of these must hold (kv_cache_interface.py:1125-1146):

query_start % hash_block == 0
checkpoint column > initial-state column
start + hash_block ≤ ckpt
start < ckpt < end
(ckpt-start) % 16 == 0 (FlashKDA alignment)

Here ckpt = ((n-1)//hash)*hash, minus one unit with EAGLE block drop (:1110-1122). The scheduler then also requires end ≥ prefill_end (scheduler.py:488-500).
Q8. A user runs P/D with prefill TP2 and decode DP2/TP1, with prefix caching on the decoder. What happens, and which env var does the test set for P/D in general? Why?
A. The test disables decoder prefix caching, because NIXL rejects it on a hybrid model with a different TP. The guard is the physical_blocks_per_logical mismatch for Mamba (base_worker.py:2467-2479; test :159-163). P/D sets VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS so that the Q/K/V conv sub-projections are contiguous per rank for the hetero-TP 3-read (ssm_conv_transfer_utils.py:1-15). DS layout also disables the FlashInfer fused decode and spec paths (kda.py:215,243).
Q9. Why is the routed-expert up-projection in latent MoE replicated rather than row/column-parallel, and what does that buy at decode?
A. With a replicated 3584→7168 weight, each rank can all-reduce [latent partial | shared partial] in one collective, then up-project and add the shared output locally with no second collective. The shared output is folded into the GEMM beta-add (model.py:304-333,665-676). For prefill, LatentMoERunner switches to a column-parallel tier that reads the same weight as a row shard, at 1/tp of the FLOPs (latent_moe_runner.py:25-51).
Q10. Why does KimiLinearModel.forward return pre-norm hidden states and apply model.norm in compute_logits? What does K3 hand EAGLE3/DFlash as an aux state under AttnRes?

Q10. Why does KimiLinearModel.forward return pre-norm hidden states and apply model.norm in compute_logits? What does K3 hand EAGLE3/DFlash as an aux state under AttnRes?
A. The MTP draft consumes pre-norm h (model.py:1413-1414,1689-1696). Under AttnRes there is no single residual stream, so aux capture returns either the prefix sum (default) or, with VLLM_KIMI_K3_AUX_ATTN_RES_STREAM=1, the AttnRes mixture that the next layer would consume, computed with that layer’s self_attention_res_{norm,proj} (:1246-1281; #50487). This mixture cannot cross a PP boundary (:1226-1232,1268).
Q11 (bonus). Which slots does the KDA metadata builder use for a spec batch with RecoverSSM, and why can one CUDA graph replay any mix of 1..k+1 query lengths?
A. It uses spec_state_slots=1 (only the checkpoint slot, kda_metadata.py:323,550-552). The builder declares AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS. KDA reads per-request offsets from the device query_start_loc within a fixed k+1 window, and padding rows are staged with NULL_BLOCK_ID and num_accepted=1 (:303-306,624-648).

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen4Exp)
Grill questions (with answer keys)


Q: Does QSA reduce KV-cache memory? Count bytes per token per QSA layer, bf16, TP1.
A: No; it reduces decode reads. Main KV is a full FullAttentionSpec: 2 heads × 256 × 2 × 2 B = 2 KiB/token. The side cost is +64 B/token compressed index key plus a fixed ring (qsa.py:543-551; qsa_cache.py:844-876).
At 262k context the indexer scans 65,536 × 256 B = 16 MiB per layer per decode step, versus about 4 MiB for the 2051 selected KV rows. So the indexer dominates at long context, which is why fp8 indexer KV (#54890) matters.


Q: What exactly is pooled into a compressed index key, and at which position is RoPE applied?
A: The mean of c=4 raw (pre-norm, pre-RoPE) keys (ops/qsa.py:431). Then GemmaRMSNorm, then RoPE at the group’s first token position (ops/qsa.py:436; indexer_qsa.py:378-391). There are no learned pooling weights, unlike DSV4.1’s gated compressor.
Members of a group can come from the ring (previous chunk) or the current chunk’s raw rows (ops/qsa.py:404-428).


Q: Why can CircularBufferSpec opt out of prefix caching without breaking correctness, while NIXL still has to transfer it?
A: Prefix hits are block-aligned. block_size is a multiple of the ring capacity, which is a multiple of c, so the open group at a hit boundary is empty and nothing older is needed (qsa_cache.py:852-855; single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1251-1263).
A P/D handoff ends at an arbitrary prompt length. The decode side must close the partial group, so the ring goes in the transfer (nixl/base_worker.py:237-243).

Q: Which tokens is a query guaranteed to see?
A: Only the causal tail of its own open group, up to c−1 = 3 tokens. Everything else must win the top-512 block selection. There is no SWA branch (ops/qsa_indexer.py:241-260).
For context ≤ 2051 tokens it is dense.


Q: In the NVIDIA HC, where is attention’s output added back into the 4 streams, and with whose weights?
A: Not in the attention block. mlp_hyper_connection.combine_and_mix(x, attn_out, inj_attn) fuses the combine into the MLP-HC RMSNorm (model.py:308-311; hyperconnection.py:177-203). The injection scalars 2σ(W_inj·xn/4) were computed by attn_HC at mix time from its normalized input (hyperconnection.py:137-159).
The pending MoE output is combined only at the next layer’s attn-HC, or by the final mixer.


Q: Name three places the delayed HC tuple must be force-materialized, and why.
A:

Before PLE (model.py:275-279), because PLE adds into the multi-stream state and gates on it.
Before a deepstack visual add (model.py:538-545).
At a PP boundary (model.py:547-554), because PP transports one tensor.
The MTP PP path does the same (mtp.py:325-329).



Q: How does GR differ from DeepSeek mHC, mathematically?
A: GR has no n×n residual-mixing matrix (mHC’s Sinkhorn-projected Hres). Streams update independently as x_s += inj_s·out. The pre-mix is per-_channel sigmoid gating followed by a mean over streams (common/hyperconnection.py:203-242).
The public paper says GR “drops branch mixing” and that the gate suppresses outliers so the residual can be stored in FP8.


Q: The PLE table is about 51B params. How does a 2-way-TP, 2-way-DP deployment with embedding_across_dp look up row r?
A:

Q: The PLE table is about 51B params. How does a 2-way-TP, 2-way-DP deployment with embedding_across_dp look up row r?
A:

ETP = TP×DP = 4 vocab shards.
Each DP rank all-gathers its ids into max-size slots (_gather_dp_ids).
Each rank UVA-gathers only rows it owns and writes zeros elsewhere, then all_reduces over ETP. FP8 is reduced as int8, which is exact because each row has one owner.
Each rank then narrows to its own slot (common/ngram_embedding.py:112-153, 374-405, 512-521).
Corollary: every DP rank must enter this collective every step.



Q: Why is the PLE short-conv state a MambaSpec with tp_replicated=True, and what does that do to page sizing and to P/D?
A:

The conv runs on the 4H = 10240 multi-stream channels after a replicated kv_proj (disable_tp=True, ple_layer.py:104-113). Every rank therefore holds the whole state (model.py:822-827).
Shape: [10240, (4−1)·3 + num_spec].
It does not shrink with TP. The platform takes the max across both Mamba specs (platforms/interface.py:1044-1050), so the PLE can set the Mamba page size at high TP or num_spec.
NIXL copies it whole from one rank, with its own _ple_block_len (#59997).



Q: With index_share_for_mtp_iteration=True, what does MTP step k ≥ 1 still compute in the QSA layer, and what does it skip?
A: It still runs the projections and writes the main KV, the ring and the compressed keys (the prepare path runs before the skip_topk check, indexer_qsa.py:298-412). It skips scoring and top-k, and reuses topk_indices_buffer rows from step 0, which compact_topk_indices compacts to target-aligned rows (mtp.py:258-269).
The valid-count column lives inside each row, so reuse and compaction keep row and count together (qsa.py:510-523).

Bonus Q: What is the hetero-TP rule for P/D of this model?
A: Both sides must be on the same side of total_kv_heads = 2: TP < 2 versus TP ≥ 2 (nixl/base_worker.py:967-989). The cause is that main KV and QSA side pages are packed per block (B-outer layout, qsa_cache.py:753-756) and move as whole blocks.


Bonus Q: Where does the 51B come from?
A: 16 hash heads ((3−1) × 8) × a prime just above 20M rows each × head_dim 2560/16 = 160 ≈ 51.2B (ngram_embedding.py:118-199; config defaults in the original config.py).

ReplaySSM
Grill questions (with answer key)


On a non-flush step, which HBM traffic does Triton ReplaySSM eliminate, and why is the kernel ceiling ~2×?
It eliminates the full-state store. S_0 is still loaded every step for S_0·C (selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only.py:317-331). The store happens only in the flush branch (:458). Traffic is about R + W/L + ring ≈ 0.55× of R+W.


Why is B·C precomputed per group in a separate kernel, and why does that kernel launch even when every row flushes?
k_jᵀq is per group, so there is a 16× reuse for 128 heads / 8 groups (:25-118). It always launches because a host-side branch can’t be captured in a CUDA graph. Flush rows self-skip instead (:65-68, :602-604).


Triton, L=16, request just admitted with a 100-token prompt. At which decode step is the first state write, and what is write_pos at num_computed=117?
decode_base = 100 (gpu_input_batch.py:387-390), so write_pos = (num_computed−100) mod 16 and the first flush is at num_computed=115 (write_pos 15, mamba_attn.py:570-573). At 117, write_pos = 1 in none mode. In align mode with block 16, the anchor is max(100,112)=112, so write_pos=5 (tests/v1/attention/test_replayssm_metadata_builder.py:119-121).


Why does FlashInfer need a ring of L+1 (or L+1+K) rows while Triton uses L?
Triton folds the current token into the flush and never stores row L−1. FlashInfer replays up to prev ≤ L committed rows plus appends the T current rows before host bookkeeping moves ring_start. So live rows reach L+T (mamba_utils.py:243-246; FI doc: logical window = RING_BUFFER_LEN − T).

Why does FlashInfer need a ring of L+1 (or L+1+K) rows while Triton uses L?
Triton folds the current token into the flush and never stores row L−1. FlashInfer replays up to prev ≤ L committed rows plus appends the T current rows before host bookkeeping moves ring_start. So live rows reach L+T (mamba_utils.py:243-246; FI doc: logical window = RING_BUFFER_LEN − T).


Under MTP, why is the tracker commit done by the first layer and the standard-decode advance by the last layer?
The commit consumes the previous step’s acceptance and must precede every layer’s read. The advance mutates cursors the current step reads, so it must follow the last layer. Trackers are shared per KV-cache group (mamba_mixer2.py:1152-1215, :908-935, :1039).


How is a rejected draft token “rolled back” for the SSM state and for the conv state?
SSM: nothing to do. Its ring row lies past ring_start+prev, and the commit adds only num_accepted (ssu_dispatch.py:111-124). No per-draft state exists (abstract.py:77-83). Conv: causal_conv1d_update(num_accepted_tokens=…) as in the baseline (mixer2:937-952).


Why are trackers per KV-cache group and not global or per layer?
Slot indices are a per-group namespace: different groups may give the same request different block IDs (mixer2:1155-1164). Per layer would be redundant, since all layers in a group advance identically.


Why is --use-replayssm incompatible with P/D disaggregation and KV offload, and what would you need to fix it?
ssm_state is a stale checkpoint between flushes. The true state is checkpoint + ring + cursor, and the cursor is not in the page (CPU decode_base for Triton, GPU trackers for FI). Validator: config/vllm.py:3430-3437. A fix would either force a flush before save/transfer or ship the rings plus cursors and re-anchor decode_base/trackers on load.

Why is --use-replayssm incompatible with P/D disaggregation and KV offload, and what would you need to fix it?

all four papers attack the same defect in one drafter (DFlash), and three of the four fixes compile down to the same Triton kernel in vLLM.
checked against vLLM main at c059bee (2026-10-11) and the xPress PR head 95ea953 (2026-10-08). the vllm-dev Slack connector was unavailable during research, so this note draws no claims from Slack. paper numbers are as the authors report them; nothing was re-run.

0. the one problem
a block-diffusion drafter (DFlash) emits B−1 tokens in one forward pass. each slot s gets a marginal qs(· | ctx), trained with per-slot cross-entropy. the target verifies conditionally: slot s survives only if it agrees with p(· | ctx, x̂<s).
so the drafter ships a product of marginals, ∏ qs, and gets graded against a chain of conditionals, ∏ p(x_s | x<s). when the marginal at slot s is bimodal (“the cat” vs “a dog”), independent argmax happily emits “the dog”, and everything after the first incoherent seam is wasted verify compute. the blog folklore name for the visible symptom is stutter: adjacent slots pick the same token.
the joint over a block is V^B, so nobody models it directly. every method below is a different bet on where to buy back the conditional dependence, and how much serial depth to pay for it:

all of them run on Model Runner V2 (vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/). DFlash, DFlash2, LiLiCorr and xPress share one forward (DFlashSpeculator._run_model) and differ only in _generate_draft.

4. cross-cutting things the papers don’t say out loud
4.1 DFlash2 and LiLiCorr are one algorithm family in vLLM. they share CandidateSampler and _selector_walk_kernel. the only difference at serve time is the function that fills a [reqs, B−1, K, K] score tensor. DFlash2’s is an einsum over token codebooks; LiLiCorr’s is a small lattice transformer over all (B−1)×K nodes. that makes the head-to-head experiment nobody has published (same target, same DFlash backbone, swap DFlash2 selector / LiLiCorr / xPress) a config change plus three checkpoints.
4.2 losslessness over a K-support proposal. under sampling, the walk draws cs from softmax over the K candidates’ edge scores given the _sampled predecessor. that conditional is the draft distribution q, and its support is only K tokens. vLLM caches exactly that: _cache_draft_logits_kernel writes the realized scores into draft_logits with −inf everywhere else, in fp32 “so the walk and the rejection that checks it read the same distribution.” rejection then uses min(1, p/q) and resamples from (p−q)+. it stays exact because q is the true proposal distribution, however narrow its support. xPress skips all this by being greedy (q one-hot).
4.3 the “40× fewer parameters” claim is a rank choice, not a structural win. DFlash2’s selector holds two vocab×rank codebooks, the same shape as DSpark’s markov_w1/markov_w2. the shipped Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint has selector_rank=256, vocab 248,320 → ≈127M selector params, ~6% of the 2B drafter. the blog’s “+2.0M params” was the Qwen3-4B ablation, which must have used a much smaller rank (inferred from arithmetic: 2 × 151,936 × r ≈ 2M → r ≈ 6–7). the real structural win is compute: DFlash2 gathers K rows per slot and scores K² edges in parallel; DSpark projects r→V per slot, serially.

4.4 what actually separates the DFlash2 selector from DSpark-with-top-K. set dspark_draft_topk=16 and DSpark also only scores 16 candidates per slot. what’s left: (i) DFlash2’s transition is gated by the slot’s hidden state H(h_t), DSpark’s bias depends on the previous token alone; (ii) DFlash2 precomputes every K×K edge before walking, DSpark computes slot s only after sampling s−1. (ii) is free here because the predecessor is always in the previous slot’s top-K anyway.
4.5 everything collapses at high concurrency. DFlash2 27B: 3.43× → ~1.0–1.45× at c=32. DFlow c=32: 1.03–1.13×. DFlash alone dips below 1.0×. once the target’s verify forward is compute-bound, every rejected token is a wasted FLOP; that’s the regime DSpark’s confidence-scheduled verification is built for, and vLLM only wires adaptive verification for DSpark (LiLiCorr docs: “shares the acceptance-estimation path, not validated”).
4.6 the benchmarks don’t overlap. LiLiCorr: Qwen3 4B/8B, H100, SGLang, 1.4M Nemotron examples. DFlow: Qwen3 1.7–8B, A800, 80K ShareGPT. xPress: Qwen3-8B, H200, vLLM. DFlash2: Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.8-27B / Muse Glimmer, H200, SGLang, no training recipe published. LiLiCorr and DFlow never cite DFlash2; DFlash2 never cites LiLiCorr or xPress. treat every cross-paper ratio as ±a lot.

5. open questions worth chasing

LiLiCorr drops the unary term from the final score; DFlash2 keeps it. which one degrades more gracefully when the drafter’s top-1 is already right (easy text, e.g. GSM8K)?
xPress’s mixer is full lower-triangular, so one pass can move information across the whole block; why does it still need K=6 passes rather than 2? (hint: the Markov bias is fed tokens, and a token at slot k only stabilizes once slot k−1 has.)
DFlow on LiLiCorr: the lattice is rebuilt each round from scratch. could the rejected-suffix lattice (not just hidden states) be relayed?
does any of this survive MoE targets at production batch? DSpark is the only one with a production claim (DeepSeek-V4).
Slack: whether Ben Chislett / the spec-decode SIG has a stated preference between LiLiCorr and DFlash2 as the default DFlash-family head. couldn’t check from here.

#27743 [KVConnector][Core] Support cross-layer KV blocks
vllm-project/vllm#27743 · orozery · MERGED · created 2025-10-29T12:27:23Z · merged 2025-11-20T18:09:59Z
Core of RFC #27742.
Following this PR, connectors can turn-on and adapt to the new layout.
This PR enables the GPU model runner to allocate the KV cache tensors, so that the KV data for all layers will be contiguous per block. This can yield a significant speed up the transfer time of KV transfers (e.g. X4), such in the case of using NixlConnector or OffloadingConnector. Currently, this new layout is disabled by default, and will only be enabled when using a connector which explicitly prefers this new layout. Also, this new layout is currently only supported for uniform (non HMA) models.

Purpose
Fixes #37032
MLA models (e.g., GLM-4.7-Flash) produce garbage output with --kv-offloading-size because cross-layer KV cache allocation creates non-contiguous per-layer views. MLA decode kernels assume contiguous block layout, so they read wrong memory for block_id > 0.

offloading_connector.py: register_kv_caches() uses AttentionLayerBase instead of Attention to match both Attention and MLAAttention layers.

Stride Order: Logical Shape vs Physical Layout
The semantic shape is always [layer_slots, blocks, heads, states, <content>]. The physical layout (memory order) is controlled by a stride_order permutation.
LBHNC (default, hetero-TP-friendly):

Logical:   [L, B, H, N, C]
Physical:  [L, B, H, N, C]  (identity)

Stride Order: Logical Shape vs Physical Layout
The semantic shape is always [layer_slots, blocks, heads, states, <content>]. The physical layout (memory order) is controlled by a stride_order permutation.
LBHNC (default, hetero-TP-friendly):

Logical:   [L, B, H, N, C]
Physical:  [L, B, H, N, C]  (identity)
stride_order = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)

Head slices are contiguous in memory. Good for head-level TP transfers, hetero-TP disagg.
LBNHC (hetero-block-size-friendly):

Logical:   [L, B, H, N, C]
Physical:  [L, B, N, H, C]
stride_order = (0, 1, 3, 2, 4)

State slices are contiguous in memory. Good for block-level transfers, hetero-block-size disagg.
BLHNC (larger P/D transfers when homo-TP/block-size):

Logical:   [L, B, H, N, C]
Physical:  [B, L, H, N, C]
stride_order = (1, 0, 2, 3, 4)

All layers’ data for one block is contiguous. The connector can transfer an entire block across all layers in a single RDMA read.
BHLNC (larger P/D transfers for hetero-TP):

Logical:   [L, B, H, N, C]
Physical:  [B, H, L, N, C]
stride_order = (1, 2, 0, 3, 4)

For a given block and head, all layers are contiguous. One contiguous region per (block, head) across all layers.

Layout constraints for shared tensors: When using HMA and groups share the same underlying KVCacheTensor (because they have the same page_size_bytes), the layers in that tensor may have different H, N, or C dimensions. In that case:

The per-layer-per-block content, [H, N, C], must be contiguous in physical memory (i.e. assert layout[0, 0, ...].is_contiguous()  # [0, 0, H, N, C]). This rules out LBNHC and BHLNC; only LBHNC and BLHNC satisfy this constraint.
If the H, N, and C sizes match across all layers in the tensor, any layout (including LBNHC and BHLNC) is valid.

For example, DeepSeek V4 has mixed compression ratios producing layers with different N and C sizes sharing a tensor — the default LBHNC layout handles this correctly.

Each spec subclass knows how to slice its own tensor. The signature takes the other spec so it can compute the correct overlap — GQA slices by heads, Mamba slices by x/B/C components, MLA may be a single unsliced latent.
GQA Slicing
Head slicing handling replication on either side (or both)

def slice_for_tp_transfer(
  self, src_tensor, src_tp, src_rank, dst_spec, dst_tp, dst_rank
):
 
  src_heads = src_tp * self.num_heads
  dst_heads = dst_tp * dst_spec.num_heads
 
  if dst_heads > src_heads:
    dst_rank %= src_tp
  elif src_rank >= dst_tp:
    return []
 
  head_range = lambda tp_rank, num_heads: (
    tp_rank * num_heads,
    (tp_rank + 1) * num_heads,
  )
 
  src_head_range = head_range(src_rank, self.num_heads)
  dst_head_range = head_range(dst_rank, dst_spec.num_heads)
 
  overlap = get_overlap(src_head_range, dst_head_range)
  if overlap is None:
    return []
 
  # Convert global overlap to local tensor indices
  local_slice = slice(
    overlap.start - src_head_range[0], overlap.stop - src_head_range[0]
  )
  return [src_tensor[:, :, local_slice]]
 
 
def get_overlap(range1, range2):
  # Calculate the intersection boundaries
  overlap_start = max(range1[0], range2[0])
  overlap_end = min(range1[1], range2[1])
 
  # Check if the boundaries form a valid range
  if overlap_start <= overlap_end:
    return slice(overlap_start, overlap_end)
  return None
Mamba Conv Slicing: 3 Slices for x/B/C

def slice_for_tp_transfer(
  self, my_tensor, my_tp, my_rank, other_spec, other_tp, other_rank
):
  # tensor: [layers, blocks, 1, 1, conv_dim/tp, kernel-1]
  x_range = self._compute_x_range(my_tp, my_rank, other_tp, other_rank)
  b_range = self._compute_b_range(my_tp, my_rank, other_tp, other_rank)
  c_range = self._compute_c_range(my_tp, my_rank, other_tp, other_rank)
  return [
    my_tensor[:, :, 0, 0, x_range, :],  # x slice
    my_tensor[:, :, 0, 0, b_range, :],  # B slice
    my_tensor[:, :, 0, 0, c_range, :],  # C slice
  ]
Same interface — spec knows its own structure.

Connector Becomes Generic
The connector needs both source and destination specs — if they have different stride orders (e.g., prefill uses HND, decode uses NHD), the source and destination slices map to different physical memory regions. Both specs produce slices in the same semantic order, so they pair directly. No backend-specific code in the connector.

#45111 [Attention] Re-enable cross-layer KV cache layout for MLA via stride-aware kernels
vllm-project/vllm#45111 · ivanium · MERGED · created 2026-06-10T06:54:30Z · merged 2026-06-22T13:57:03Z
Purpose
#37090 disabled the cross-layer (block-major) KV cache layout for all MLA backends after #37032 (GLM-4.7-Flash garbage output with KV offloading), attributing the bug to “MLA kernels requiring contiguous per-layer KV cache views”. The actual cause is narrower: a few kernels computed page addresses from block_size * entry_size instead of reading the cache tensor’s block-dim stride. The MLA write path (concat_and_cache_mla), the prefill gather kernels (cp_gather_cache, gather_and_maybe_dequant_cache), DeepGEMM fp8_paged_mqa_logits, and several decode kernels are already stride-aware.
This PR fixes the three kernels that genuinely assumed packed pages and re-enables the cross-layer layout per backend (opt-in), keeping the safe identity default on MLACommonBackend for backends not yet verified (ROCm AITER, tokenspeed, XPU).
Kernel fixes

vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_decode_attention.py: both stage-1 decode kernels addressed the cache as (page_number * PAGE_SIZE + offset) * stride(-3), baking in stride(block) == PAGE_SIZE * stride(token). They now take the page-dim stride separately. This is the kernel behind the original #37032 report (A100 falls back to TRITON_MLA).
csrc/libtorch_stable/attention/mla/sm100_cutlass_mla_kernel.cu: stride_C hardcoded page_size * (D_latent + D_rope); now built from kv_c_and_k_pe_cache.stride(0)/stride(1) (identical values for contiguous caches).
csrc/libtorch_stable/cache_kernels.cu indexer_k_quant_and_cache: block base was block_idx * cache_block_size * kv_cache.size(2); now block_idx * kv_cache.stride(0). Writing through a strided view previously corrupted the target layer and bled into neighbouring layers’ segments. This also unblocks the DeepSeek V3.2/V4 indexer KV cache group under packed/cross-layer layouts.

Per-backend opt-in
get_kv_cache_stride_order(include_num_layers_dimension=True) returns (1, 0, 2, 3) on backends whose decode kernels verifiably honor the cache’s block-dim stride: TritonMLA and CutlassMLA (fixed above), FlashAttnMLA (FA3 reads k_batch_stride = kcache.stride(0)), FlashMLA (dense decode reads kcache.stride(0)), and FlashInferMLA (verified bit-exact). MLACommonBackend keeps the identity permutation as the safe default, so unverified backends remain opted out and can opt in individually once verified.
Tests
tests/kernels/attention/test_mla_cross_layer_kernel_equivalence.py (new) runs each kernel on a contiguous cache vs a per-layer view carved from a cross-layer buffer (inflated stride(0), non-zero storage offset, neighbour layers filled with garbage) and asserts bit-exact equality: concat_and_cache_mla write (incl. zero bleed), FlashMLA dense decode (Hopper-gated), FlashMLA dense fp8 decode (Hopper-gated), FA3 decode (Hopper-gated), FlashInfer MLA dense decode (bf16 + fp8), FlashMLA fp8 sparse decode, and indexer_k_quant_and_cache (incl. zero bleed). Similar strided-view tests are added for the triton decode kernels (all three address paths: MLA grouped, GQA grouped, MHA normal) and CUTLASS sm100 MLA decode. The MLA stride-order unit tests are updated for the opt-in design.
Why this is not duplicating an existing PR
Searched open PRs for cross-layer/stride-order work: #44577 packs DSv4 KV caches into contiguous per-block allocations but only touches allocation/connector/runner plumbing, no kernels — this PR is complementary (the kernel stride fixes here are what make such packed per-block layouts safe for MLA decode/write kernels). #41093 adds cross-layer support on the Mooncake connector side only. The KV-layout refactor series (#44458 draft, #44455, #42374) standardizes layout plumbing and overlaps some files but does not address the packed-page stride bugs or the MLA cross-layer opt-ins. #34742 is the stride-order default refactor referenced in #37090 review and is orthogonal.

# 118 passed (incl. new cross-layer strided-view tests; no regression in existing paged/fp8 paths)

#46116 [Core][KV-transfer] MoRIIO: heterogeneous TP←>DP prefill/decode read routing
vllm-project/vllm#46116 · edwinlim0919 · MERGED · created 2026-06-18T23:59:08Z · merged 2026-07-27T02:10:00Z
Part of RFC #46107.
Purpose
MoRIIO today assumes the prefill and decode engines share the same parallelism layout. This PR enables heterogeneous disaggregated prefill/decode, where the two phases run different parallelism (TP vs DP+EP). The performance results in the RFC which encompasses this PR shows that heterogeneous parallel PD setups can achieve higher throughput and lower TTFT at high concurrency levels than their homogeneous parallel PD counterparts on MI300X (gfx942). This PR contains the support for both mixed-parallel configurations below:

Forward: P_DP8EP → D_TP8 (DP/EP prefill, TP decode)
Mirror: P_TP8 → D_DP8EP (TP prefill, DP/EP decode)

Forward: P_DP8EP → D_TP8 (DP/EP prefill, TP decode)
Mirror: P_TP8 → D_DP8EP (TP prefill, DP/EP decode)

Three focused changes, one per commit:
1. Read from the request’s prefill DP rank, not hardcoded DP0
Previously the READ path resolved the remote session and read-completion notify port from a hardcoded prefill DP rank 0, regardless of which prefill DP rank actually computed the KV. Under heterogeneous DP prefill the proxy forwards the owning rank in kv_transfer_params["remote_dp_rank"]; the read now targets it. remote_dp_rank == 0 (the symmetric single-DP case) is byte-identical to prior behaviour.
2. Eager pre-forward handshake (deadlock fix)
A decode TP worker reads from whichever prefill rank owns each request, so across requests every worker must reach several remote ranks. The previous lazy per-rank handshake on the read path lets the TP workers diverge. One rank can race ahead into a forward collective (TP all-gather, or the DP+EP all-to-all on the decode side) while a peer is still blocked in a handshake recv() → 600s NCCL timeout / hang. We handshake every referenced remote rank up front in start_load_kv, once per engine, behind a CPU all_reduce(MIN) barrier so all workers finish together and fail fast + uniformly on error.
3. Flexible prefill-TP read (mirror)
For a TP-replicated prefill + MLA feeding a DP decode, the latent KV is replicated across every prefill TP rank, so any is a valid source. Instead of every decode DP rank funnelling onto prefill tp0 (a single-GPU NIC bottleneck), each decode rank round-robins its reads across tp0..N-1 to spread the RDMA/prefill-NIC load. The choice is gated (all four must hold, so non-mirror configs are untouched):

world_size == 1: decode is TP1, no local TP collective to keep in lockstep;
use_mla: latent KV replicated across prefill TP ranks → any rank valid;
remote_dp_size == 1: pure-TP prefill (no DP partition constraining source);
remote_tp_size > 1: more than one prefill TP rank to spread across.

world_size == 1: decode is TP1, no local TP collective to keep in lockstep;
use_mla: latent KV replicated across prefill TP ranks → any rank valid;
remote_dp_size == 1: pure-TP prefill (no DP partition constraining source);
remote_tp_size > 1: more than one prefill TP rank to spread across.

Outside the gate the source rank is the fixed local-rank mapping (_remote_tp_rank), byte-identical to prior behaviour. The chosen rank is threaded identically through the (dp, tp) session key, the handshake dial, and the notify port, so a read and its completion notify always address the same prefill rank. A drift would read one rank but notify another, leaving that rank’s prefill buffer unfreed (KV leak → MR overflow).
The round-robin is deterministic (staggered by the decode rank’s dp_rank), not random: it gives exactly-uniform NIC spread and is trivially testable.

#46332 [ROCm][P/D] Support MoRIIO heterogeneous TP fan-in
vllm-project/vllm#46332 · tanpinsiang · MERGED · created 2026-06-22T03:18:33Z · merged 2026-06-23T10:33:24Z
Summary
This PR builds on the MoRIIO typed control-message support merged in #46290.
This PR adds MoRIIO READ-mode support for heterogeneous prefill/decode TP sizes, e.g. P4/D8 and P8/D4.
Changes

Add remote TP rank mapping for local_tp != remote_tp.
Use the mapped TP rank for MoRIIO handshake and READ release notify ports.
Send READ release ACKs as typed msgpack release messages with consumer_tp_size.
Count producer-side ACK fan-in before reporting finished_sending.
Preserve duplicate release ACKs instead of deduping them.
Guard unsupported heterogeneous-TP KV head splitting.
Add focused unit coverage for rank mapping, ACK fan-in, stale ACKs, duplicate ACKs, and head-splitting guard.

Notes
This refactors READ completion ACKs to use the typed msgpack control-message path introduced in #46290. Plain string completions are still accepted for backward compatibility and are treated as a single ACK.

@vllmellm @hongxiayang @junkang1991 @tanpinsiang @chunfangamd @TianDi101 @functionstackx @tjtanaa.

#47572 [RFC]: ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs instead of state for faster standard and speculative decode (Mamba2 + GDN)
vllm-project/vllm#47572 · Johnny-Liou · OPEN · created 2026-07-03T19:56:53Z
Motivation.
Summary
ReplaySSM is a memory-bandwidth optimization for the decode kernels of state space model (SSM) and linear attention layers. It is a collaboration between Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA; a concurrent cross-framework implementation is in the TensorRT-LLM PR.
SSM decode is memory-bound: today each step reads and writes back the full recurrent state. ReplaySSM instead caches recent inputs, reconstructing the state only when needed and otherwise computing the output directly from the cache. This keeps most steps read-only and writes the full state back only once every L steps.
ReplaySSM provides three benefits:

Memory-traffic reduction in a bandwidth-bound kernel: the per-step state write is replaced by a small input append.
Cheap rollback for speculative decoding: caching recent SSM inputs makes rollback a buffer pointer move, avoiding the separate per-draft-token state the current implementation keeps.
Parallel verification for speculative decoding: on non-flush steps the output is read directly without materializing the state, so a draft window is verified in one shot instead of by a serial recurrence.

Implementation: we have opened a draft PR (#47576) implementing ReplaySSM in vLLM, based on the ReplaySSM reference repository.
We are aware of the existing feature request #46187, which tracks ReplaySSM in vLLM and is assigned to us as the ReplaySSM authors. This RFC and the accompanying draft PR are the upstream contribution we committed to.
Motivation
Two problems motivate ReplaySSM.

In hybrid models, the SSM (linear-attention) layers are the decode bottleneck at short-to-medium output lengths (Fig 2 in the blog post). SSM decode is memory-bound and its per-step state read/write dominates HBM traffic.
Speculative decoding must roll back rejected draft tokens, but the SSM state update is irreversible: once history is summarized into the recurrent state, a token cannot be subtracted back out. To support rollback, the current implementation keeps a separate recurrent state per draft token, which costs extra memory traffic and extra HBM footprint (about (1 + num_spec)× the state), hurting both latency and maximum concurrency.

ReplaySSM addresses both by caching inputs instead of state. It keeps a single checkpoint state S0 and caches the recent SSM inputs in a ring buffer; on a flush step (once every L steps) it folds the cached inputs into the checkpoint, and on every other step it computes the output directly from the checkpoint plus the cached inputs without materializing the full state.
For standard decode, writing the state back only once every L steps (instead of every step) roughly halves the dominant memory traffic. For speculative decode, caching recent inputs makes rollback a ring-buffer pointer move, cutting the per-step rollback cost from O(T) to O(1) (T = num_spec_tokens + 1) and removing the per-draft-token state storage, which improves both latency and maximum concurrency.
ReplaySSM speeds up the SSM kernel most at large serving batch sizes, where the kernel is fully memory-bound (small batch is not a relevant operating point: there the kernel is overhead-bound rather than memory-bound, and e2e latency is dominated by the MLP layers). For hybrid models it gives the largest end-to-end speedup at short-to-medium output lengths, where the SSM layers dominate latency.
Proposed Change.
Proposed Change
We propose adding ReplaySSM to vLLM as an opt-in decode path for hybrid SSM models, covering both SSM families and both decode modes, with the baseline path unchanged when the feature is off.
Scope

Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) SSM layers.
Standard and speculative decode.
New Triton kernels plus the vLLM integration (mixer dispatch, attention-metadata cursors, state-shape sizing). The conv path reuses vLLM’s existing causal_conv1d_update unchanged.

The feature is opt-in through config flags that all default to off; when off, the decode path is byte-for-byte the baseline. The ReplaySSM caches are added as extra tensors on the existing paged mamba state, so they reuse vLLM’s paged-block allocation and block-table indexing (continuous batching, per-request allocation and eviction).

Core concept

SSM decode is memory-bound: each step loads and stores a (nheads, d, n) recurrent state; the state store dominates traffic.
ReplaySSM keeps a small ring buffer of recent inputs and a periodic checkpoint state; it reconstructs the state (or reads the output directly) from the checkpoint + buffer, and writes the full state back only on periodic flushes.

Less memory traffic: halves the dominant state traffic in standard decode (state store replaced by a small input append most steps).

Parallel verification: most steps only need the output, not the state: the output-only form computes all T draft outputs from one checkpoint + buffer in a single GEMM (removing the length-T serial recurrence), and materializes the full state only at a flush.

A single checkpoint state S₀, loaded every step and written back only on flushes (see below), replacing the baseline’s per-step state store.
Conv state reuses vLLM’s causal_conv1d_update unchanged; in spec decode the window is conv_kernel-1+num_spec and rollback is a shift keyed on num_accepted_tokens. ReplaySSM never touches the conv path.


When we flush (write the checkpoint): B (--replayssm-buffer-len, default 16) is the maximum number of history tokens (past SSM inputs) the buffer holds. A flush reconstructs the recurrent state from the cached history tokens and writes it back as the new checkpoint S₀ in HBM; the history window then restarts.

Standard: each step appends one input to the size-B buffer, so we flush every B steps.
Speculative: a verify step consumes a window of T = num_spec_tokens + 1 tokens at once, so we flush whenever history_tokens + T > B (the next window would not fit). This guarantees every verify step has room for a full T-draft window, preventing window collapse / truncation.


Ring-buffer sizing (spec): the ring holds L = B + T slots. A flush step carries at most B history tokens (from the flush rule above) and appends the current window of up to T, so L = B + T always has room for a full T-draft window on top of the history, so the window never collapses or truncates.

Physical size: we currently round the logical size up to next_pow2(L) so wraparound indexing is a cheap bit-mask (& (N-1)) instead of a % L. Sizing the ring to exactly L = B + T (dropping the pow2 slack to save cache memory) is future work.

Why a ring buffer (spec): the number of accepted tokens is only known after the whole step, so rejected drafts must be discarded cheaply. Rather than relocate accepted tokens to the front of the buffer every layer/step, the kernel indexes the cache circularly and moves cursors instead of data.

Circular indexing (in-kernel): every cache access maps to physical slot (post_origin + write_pos + offs) & (buf - 1), driven by two block-keyed cursors: post_origin (the window’s circular base) and write_pos (committed-history offset).
Commit / rollback (device-side, no data movement): a normal step does write_pos += num_accepted (rejected drafts are never committed, which is the rollback); a flush advances post_origin past the committed history and resets write_pos.

The problem: whether a row flushes (is_flush) is per-row runtime data that varies across the batch (continuous batching) and across steps (variable acceptance), so the host cannot pick the launch set.
The solution: the launch sequence stays fixed. Every step issues both a verify launch and a flush launch; each kernel is compiled for its single role (is_flush is a compile-time constant per launch), and every row early-exits from the launch that does not apply to it. Which rows flush is routed on-device by the is_flush flags, not by host slicing.
The result: since the commit and flush-decision also run on-device (no host sync on num_accepted), the launch sequence is identical every step, so one captured graph per batch size covers the whole decode path.


Paged cache layout: all ReplaySSM caches live inside the paged KV block, not in registers or a private per-request buffer, for two reasons. First, they are live across decode steps: the checkpoint persists until the next flush and the input ring accumulates history over many steps, so they must sit in HBM between kernel launches. Second, vLLM addresses every per-request recurrent state through paged blocks and a block table (continuous batching, variable active-request sets, prefix caching); we append our caches as extra tensors on the baseline (conv, ssm) state so they reuse that machinery, indexed per request by physical block id and allocated/freed with the request. Only the small per-block cursors (write_pos, post_origin, is_flush) for spec live in the metadata builder rather than the page.

What we page (never the read/query vector): the output’s read vector (Mamba2 C, GDN q) is never cached in any mode; it comes from the current step’s activations. Only the state-building inputs are paged:

Mamba2: x, B, dt. Standard uses separate size-B caches; spec packs x|B plus dt in a circular next_pow2(B+T) ring. C is read fresh from conv_out.
GDN: (d, k, g), where d is the corrected update u. Standard uses size-B caches; spec uses a circular next_pow2(B+T) ring. q is read fresh.

Mamba2: x, B, dt. Standard uses separate size-B caches; spec packs x|B plus dt in a circular next_pow2(B+T) ring. C is read fresh from conv_out.
GDN: (d, k, g), where d is the corrected update u. Standard uses size-B caches; spec uses a circular next_pow2(B+T) ring. q is read fresh.


The only structural difference across families and modes is the buffer geometry: size-B for standard, a circular next_pow2(B+T) ring for spec (room for the T-window).


Cache dtypes: the checkpoint state follows the configured SSM dtype (mamba_ssm_cache_dtype; fp32 by default for the evaluated NVFP4 models, but FP16/BF16 supported); the input-vector caches (Mamba2 x/B, GDN d/k) follow the activation dtype (bf16); the per-step scalars that drive cumulative decay (Mamba2 dt, GDN g) are always fp32, for numerically-stable decay replay (and they are tiny, no d/n dim).
