#48018 [Kernel] ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs for faster Mamba2 standard decode
vllm-project/vllm#48018 · Johnny-Liou · MERGED · created 2026-07-08T16:10:51Z · merged 2026-07-24T16:39:50Z
Background
This is the first sub-PR split out from the large draft PR #47576, which presents the full ReplaySSM design across Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet for both standard and speculative decode. To keep review tractable, this PR lands only the first stage, Mamba2 standard decode. ReplaySSM caches recent SSM inputs instead of writing the recurrent state back to HBM on every step. It is a collaboration between Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA, and the full derivation and figures are in the blog post. AI assistance was used for parts of this work, and the authors have reviewed every changed line.
Core concept
SSM decode is memory-bound. Each step loads and stores a (nheads, d, n) recurrent state, and that per-step state store dominates HBM traffic. ReplaySSM keeps a small ring buffer of recent inputs together with a periodic checkpoint state. On most steps it reads the decode output directly from the checkpoint plus the buffer, without materializing the full state, and it writes the full state back only on periodic flushes, once every L steps, where L is the buffer length. On the non-flush steps the per-step state store becomes a small input append, which roughly halves the dominant traffic.
The baseline only becomes bandwidth-bound at large batch. The table below reports the DRAM bandwidth the baseline selective_state_update reaches, as a percentage of peak, at the tuned config and measured in isolation.

bsH100 fp32H100 fp16B300 fp32B300 fp16121.6%13.3%9.3%4.5%863.3%43.3%32.9%24.0%3280.3%74.3%65.0%45.0%12884.2%82.2%81.7%72.5%25684.5%83.7%84.5%78.4%51284.6%84.0%85.6%81.3%
At small batch the per-request state footprint is tiny and the launch grid is small, so too few memory transactions are in flight to cover HBM latency, and the kernel is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound. In a hybrid model the small-batch step is also dominated by the MLP layers, not the SSM layers. Small batch is therefore not the target regime. ReplaySSM targets serving batch, where the SSM kernel saturates HBM and the per-step state store is the bottleneck.
What this PR adds
Everything here is opt-in. With the feature off, the decode path is byte-for-byte the baseline.

The Mamba2 output-only decode kernel selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only, plus its hardware-keyed launch-config helper.
Two config flags, both default off. --use-replayssm turns on Mamba2 standard cached decode, and --replayssm-buffer-len sets the history buffer length L (default 16).
Integration. The Mamba2 mixer dispatches to the kernel under the flag, the Mamba attention metadata builder carries the per-row ring cursor and flush flag, and the state-shape calculator sizes the extra caches on the paged state. The conv path reuses vLLM’s causal_conv1d_update unchanged.

The feature requires --mamba-cache-mode none, and it covers standard (non-speculative) decode only.
Design notes
Paged cache layout
The input ring caches (x, dt, B) and the checkpoint state live inside the paged KV block, appended as extra tensors on the baseline (conv, ssm) state. They stay live across decode steps, the checkpoint until the next flush and the ring across many steps, so they must sit in HBM between kernel launches. Appending them onto the paged state reuses vLLM’s per-request block allocation and block-table indexing directly. The output read vector (Mamba2 C) is never cached; it comes from the current step’s activations.
CUDA graphs and continuous batching
Whether a row flushes is per-row runtime data. Under continuous batching the rows in one captured batch sit at different buffer positions, so is_flush varies across the batch and cannot be a compile-time constant, even for standard decode. The kernel takes is_flush as a per-row input and branches on it inside the kernel, so one captured graph per batch size covers both the non-flush and the flush rows. The write position is decode_step mod L, computed on the host each step from scheduler token counts and copied to the device asynchronously, so no device-to-host sync is needed.
Results
Two models are evaluated, Nemotron-3-Nano-4B (BF16) on one H100 and Nemotron-3-Super-120B (NVFP4) on one B300, at buffer length 16 with fp32 and fp16 SSM state, greedy, and CUDA graphs on. End-to-end numbers are produced with benchmarks/replayssm/e2e_decode_speedup.py.

On B300, and especially at fp16, the kernel sits below the baseline ceiling because the flush reconstruction dot caps the flush-branch bandwidth. Splitting the decode kernel into two, one for the non-flush branch and one for the flush branch, raises bandwidth utilization substantially. Under CUDA graphs that split forces two launches per step, and the double-launch overhead hurts on Hopper but pays off on Blackwell. A Blackwell-specific split kernel is planned as a follow-up.
B300 also shows a power effect. The baseline draws more power than ReplaySSM and throttles its SM clock under the enforced cap, which costs bandwidth. In the full model this makes the fp32 baseline about 1.6x slower than in kernel-level isolation, while ReplaySSM keeps full clock. A higher power cap would likely close this gap.

Tests
Correctness is checked at three levels, all on Mamba2.
Per-step kernel correctness lives in tests/kernels/mamba/test_replayssm_standard_decode_mamba2.py. Every decode step is checked against an exact fp32 reference and against the baseline decode kernel, over multi-flush sequences, across six state and activation precision combinations, the production model geometries, buffer lengths 1/4/16, the z gate, and continuous batching with per-row buffer positions and null-padded slots. The file also includes a tensor-parallel head-shard equivalence check, that one monolithic run equals concatenating the independent per-rank shards. Tolerances are near-exact at fp32 (rtol 1e-4, atol 1e-3), tight enough to catch a TF32 matmul-precision regression, and looser at bf16 and fp16 where rounding dominates.

Prefill and decode equivalence lives in tests/kernels/mamba/test_replayssm_prefill_decode_equivalence_mamba2.py. Because the SSM recurrence is path-independent, the chunked prefill path and step-by-step decode must give the same per-position outputs and final state, and both are anchored on the exact recurrence.

Out of scope

The further precision benefit of ReplaySSM. Because the checkpoint is written back only on flushes, a low-precision checkpoint is quantized far less often than under the per-step baseline store. Quantifying this is still in progress.

#49226 [Bugfix][KVConnector] Disable cross-layer KV blocks for per-token-head quant
vllm-project/vllm#49226 · Achyuthan-S · MERGED · created 2026-07-20T16:42:10Z · merged 2026-07-26T02:24:28Z
Purpose
Fixes #48412.
Combining OffloadingConnector with a per-token-head quantized KV cache
(fp8_per_token_head / int8_per_token_head / int4_per_token_head) corrupts
generations on the first forward pass, before any offloaded block is ever
restored.
Root cause
OffloadingConnector.prefer_cross_layer_blocks is hardcoded True. For
single-group models on backends with indexes_kv_by_block_stride (e.g.
TRITON_ATTN), the model runner therefore allocates a cross-layer KV cache
(allocate_uniform_kv_caches in kv_connector_model_runner_mixin.py): one
contiguous buffer shared by all layers.
Per-token-head quant stores an inline fp32 scale in a padded tail of each
(head, token) cell. The attention backend carves strided fp32 views over
those pad bytes in _ensure_scale_caches (triton_attn.py), assuming a
per-layer, contiguous buffer. Against the interleaved cross-layer
allocation, the assumed block stride is wrong and every layer’s scale views
collide at the same offset, so writing scales aliases neighboring K/V data and
corrupts the cache from the first decode.
Fix
Return prefer_cross_layer_blocks = False when the KV cache dtype uses
per-token-head scales, so these models take the per-layer offload path
(which lays out each cell’s scale pad correctly). Non-per-token-head configs —
plain fp8 included — are unchanged and still prefer the cross-layer layout.
This is a soft fallback, not a hard failure: offloading still works for these
dtypes via the per-layer path — only the cross-layer transfer optimization is
skipped, and only for per-token-head dtypes. Teaching the cross-layer allocation
and _ensure_scale_caches to pack scales in the shared buffer would restore that
optimization, but is a larger, hotter-path change and can be a follow-up.

#49612 [KV Connector] Support NIXL heterogeneous P/D block sizes for hybrid models
vllm-project/vllm#49612 · njhill · MERGED · created 2026-07-23T16:06:20Z · merged 2026-07-28T13:45:03Z
Hybrid (mamba) models previously asserted out heterogeneous block sizes entirely — yet they are the models where P/D block sizes most readily diverge, since the mamba-padded attention block size varies with TP sharding (#41037). Lift the restriction:

Mamba state blocks are indivisible, so their descriptors always use local page geometry and their desc ids are never ratio-expanded; attention descriptors remain expanded to remote-block granularity.
A shared per-group mapping (pull READ and push WRITE) expands attention groups to remote granularity and clips to the transferred coverage, while mamba groups map 1:1.
The receive post-process permutes only attention-layer caches (a lazily cached list) and zeroes everything past the transferred coverage — the untransferred token tail of the last partially covered block plus any blocks beyond it — whose zeroing the scheduler skipped for the load. The clip happens at remote-block granularity with a block-size ratio, and at kernel-block granularity when equal kernel pages meet differing logical block sizes, so mamba hybrids need this zeroing even when the ratio is 1 (including MLA).
The multi-read hetero-TP path (P_TP > D_TP with sharded SSM state, #49297) builds its per-source split handles from the remote- granularity descriptors, keyed by (tp_ratio, remote_block_size); replicated and single-source attention descriptors pass through whole, and SSM chunking is unaffected by the ratio.

#49762 [KV Connector] Support NIXL P/D for hybrid MLA+SSM models
vllm-project/vllm#49762 · njhill · MERGED · created 2026-07-24T20:46:32Z · merged 2026-07-29T03:50:31Z
Re-implements the intent of vllm-project/vllm#44848 on top of the reworked NIXL connector, from the current architecture rather than the original patch. KimiLinear pools its KDA (GDN-typed MambaSpec) and MLA layers into shared HMA tensors, making every region dual-purpose. Since the mamba-page unification raises the attention block size until the MLA page equals the unified page, and FlashMLA fixes the kernel block at 64 tokens, both sides always exchange kernel-granularity geometry that is TP-independent for MLA: block_size_ratio stays 1 and TP variance is absorbed by the existing per-engine physical_blocks_per_logical handling. What remains are three real gaps:

register_kv_caches marked a shared region’s FA view by whichever layer registered it first; a KDA-first ordering left dual-purpose regions flagged as head-sharded. Merge the MLA flag on the HMA dedup path so split handles replicate their FA descriptors.
The push worker’s replicated-MLA WRITE branch asserted a single source rank, which hybrid MLA+SSM violates (sharded SSM targets every covered D rank). Replicate only the attention groups across the write ranks and route hybrid writes through the per-rank split handles, mirroring the pull side.
Handshake validation skipped all FA block_len checks for mamba models; hybrid MLA can and now does enforce the TP-independent invariant that kernel-granularity block_lens match exactly.

The KDA conv state decomposes as GDN (equal Q/K/V sub-projections), so the existing 3-read conv transfer applies unchanged. Heterogeneous physical_blocks_per_logical still requires disabling prefix caching, as already enforced at handshake time.

#49969 [Spec Decode] Add top-k DSpark Markov projection
vllm-project/vllm#49969 · askliar · MERGED · created 2026-07-27T10:28:37Z · merged 2026-08-04T12:52:53Z
Purpose
DSpark computes the base logits for all draft positions in parallel, then applies the Markov bias sequentially over the full draft vocabulary. The repeated full-vocabulary Markov projection is on the serial drafting path.
This PR adds dspark_draft_topk for Qwen3 DSpark. It selects the top-k candidates from the base logits once, gathers the corresponding markov_w2 rows, and evaluates the sequential Markov bias only for those candidates.
The current implementation deliberately reuses the existing dense sampling path:

Compute dense base logits and select the top-k candidates once for all draft positions.
Initialize the reusable dense logits buffer to -inf.
At each sequential step, apply the Markov bias only to the selected candidates and scatter the corrected values into that dense row.
Use the existing greedy or probabilistic Gumbel/rejection sampling path unchanged.

The base LM-head output and probabilistic draft-logits storage remain dense. This optimization specifically reduces the repeated sequential Markov projection while avoiding custom proposal and rejection-sampling plumbing.
Current scope:

Qwen3 DSpark

Check GSM8K accuracy and acceptance length for greedy and probabilistic drafting.
Profile the decode window to confirm that savings occur in the drafter projection.
Run focused configuration/top-k tests and repository pre-commit hooks.

Hi @gau-nernst, question on the SM100 path here.
The kernel indexes layer_res/delta/output with a hard-coded row stride of H, threading real strides only for blocks.
Nothing enforces that: the dispatch asserts stride(-1) == 1 but not stride(0) == hidden_size, and there’s no STD_TORCH_CHECK either. On a B200 build, feeding a row-padded prefix (stride(0)=7175, H=7168) gives max|out-ref| = 6.66 against the suite’s 8e-2 — no fault, no NaN, and the in-place prefix update is wrong too.
Is packed rows an intended precondition? If the K3 model never passes padded slices, I’ll send a STD_TORCH_CHECK so it fails loudly. If they’re reachable, the dispatch should decline them and fall back to Triton, which already threads the strides correctly. Happy to do either and hear your thoughts~

target layers. K3 captures the post-mixture stream, which is not what the
drafter was trained against: the AttnRes residual mixture is applied before
the layer norm, and the current capture site reads the value after it.
Tapping the pre-norm mixture instead recovers the stream the drafter expects.
This selects the correct weights to mix against depending on where the
tapped layer sits — the next layer’s own AttnRes weights when one follows,
the model’s output-side aggregation for the last layer on the final pipeline
stage, and a fall back to the running prefix for the last layer of a
non-final stage, where the consumer lives on the next rank and the
output-side weights do not exist there.
Gated behind VLLM_KIMI_K3_AUX_ATTN_RES_STREAM (default off) while it
settles, since it changes what the model feeds the speculator.
The one-shot log of which layers are tapped and which capture mode is active
is emitted from _set_aux_hidden_state_layers, the setup-time hook the
speculator calls once, rather than from inside forward. Setting an
nn.Module attribute inside a compiled forward pass risks a graph break or
recompile under torch.compile; doing it at setup time avoids that and is
also the natural place to log the tapped layer tuple.
I checked for duplicate/overlapping open PRs (gh pr list --search on “kimi k3 aux hidden state” and “attn_res eagle3”); no open PR touches the Kimi K3 auxiliary hidden state capture site. I used AI assistance (Cursor) to draft, test, and validate this change, and I reviewed every changed line before submitting.

16 layers, attn_res_block_size = 4, pp = 2
  stage 0 = layers 0..7        stage 1 = layers 8..15
  aux capture id 8, i.e. the residual stream after layer 7

Capture id 8 is stage 0’s end_layer, so this PR takes the fallback there.
What layer 8 actually reads, and what the same config captures at pp=1:

sources = [bank[0], bank[1], prefix]  # cdiv(8, 4) = 2 blocks, plus the prefix
w = softmax(
  score(s) for s in sources
)  # score uses layer 8's res_norm / res_proj
feature = w[0] * bank[0] + w[1] * bank[1] + w[2] * prefix
What gets captured at pp=2:

feature = prefix  # i.e. w hard-coded to [0, 0, 1]
The mixture is a convex combination, so returning prefix alone is the same as
forcing the softmax one-hot onto the last source and discarding bank[0] and
bank[1]. Those aren’t a remainder term — the weights are learned and generally
spread out. In a harness driving the real attn_res kernel (synthetic weights,
so illustrative), cosine similarity between the two expressions above ran 0.05
to 0.60.
The practical problem is that the same layer id now means two different things
depending on how the model is sharded, while the drafter at serving time always
consumes the first one. And it’s silent: right shape, right dtype, no NaNs.
It needs VLLM_KIMI_K3_AUX_ATTN_RES_STREAM=1 plus a capture id that coincides
with a stage end, so exposure grows with pp. For 93 layers with ids at
{8, 32, 48, 64, 88} under the default get_pp_indices, the first collision is at
pp=10 and from pp=40 on all five ids are stage ends.

prefix — local
bank — local, and stage 0’s num_attn_res_blocks is cdiv(8, 4) = 2, which
is exactly layer 8’s prev_valid_blocks, so it is already the right length
res_norm.weight / res_proj.weight — on stage 1

Those two are one hidden_size vector each, unsharded and unquantised, about
28KB together at hidden 7168.

Keep a copy of them on non-final stages. Redirect them in load_weights before

#50611 [Nixl][PD] DCP support for MLA models
vllm-project/vllm#50611 · NickLucche · MERGED · created 2026-07-31T18:30:04Z · merged 2026-08-29T16:03:54Z
Alternative to vllm-project/vllm#38433 as we iterate on the design with @pisceskkk .
I feel this version is much closer to the changes we should see to the core files in terms of code structure and modifications to the workflow - it should result closer to injecting DCP login into current abstraction, rather than building something on the side.
However, it makes some significant assumptions to do that, described below.

NIXL P/D disaggregation assumed MLA’s KV cache is fully duplicated across TP, so a remote rank only needs to be read once. Decode Context Parallel (DCP) breaks that: it shards KV by block across ranks.

  Producer  (dcp_size=4) -- KV sharded into 4 slices, one per rank
  +------+------+------+------+
  |  P0  |  P1  |  P2  |  P3  |
  +--+---+--+---+--+---+--+---+
     |      |      |      |
     v      v      v      v
  +------+------+------+------+
  |  D0  |  D1  |  D0  |  D1  |   <-  remote_rank % local_dcp_size == local_dcp_rank
  +------+------+------+------+
  Decoder   (dcp_size=2) -- each rank owns 2x the slice, reads 2 remote ranks

    D0 reads {P0, P2}   D1 reads {P1, P3}




NOTE 



Key simplifying assumption: per side, dcp_size is either 1 (fully replicated, unchanged pre-existing behavior) or tp_size (fully sharded, disjoint 1/dcp_size slice per rank) — never partial (1 < dcp_size < tp_size).

D0 reads {P0, P2}   D1 reads {P1, P3}




NOTE 



Key simplifying assumption: per side, dcp_size is either 1 (fully replicated, unchanged pre-existing behavior) or tp_size (fully sharded, disjoint 1/dcp_size slice per rank) — never partial (1 < dcp_size < tp_size).


This means DCP sharding and the old “multiple TP replicas, pick one canonically” logic never have to compose on the same side, which is what keeps the routing logic to three flat cases (both replicated / one-replicated-one-sharded / both-sharded) instead of a general partial-overlap solver.
Two supporting assumptions that follow from it:

DCP sizes across sides always divide one another (real deployments use power-of-two/highly-composite degrees) — avoids needing gcd/lcm logic, plain modulo suffices.
DCP shards at block granularity when a KV connector is attached (cp_kv_cache_interleave_size pinned to block_size) — this is quite fundamental. However I had to update a few attn backends to make sure they get the updated value.

#50649 [ROCm][Bugfix] Kimi-K3 Fix KDA NaN on mixed batches and racy autotune config
vllm-project/vllm#50649 · kliuae · MERGED · created 2026-08-01T02:45:57Z · merged 2026-08-05T08:07:22Z
Purpose
For Kimi-K3, there are two correctness bugs on the ROCm Kimi-K3 KDA path.

KimiGatedDeltaNetAttention._forward sends the decode sequences of a mixed decode+prefill non-speculative batch through the KDA chunk kernel chunk_kda_with_fused_gate. The chunk kernel treats each decode as length=1 sequence, and returns NaN for them. This PR separates the decode out of the mixed batch and pass them to fused_recurrent_kda.
recompute_w_u_fwd_kernel autotunes the configuration of num_stages=4. This configuration, particularly in combination with num_warps=4, is racy for this kernel, and can silently produce large (e.g. ~1e38) garbage values that corrupts the downstream. This PR addresses this by leaving the num_stages=4 out in autotuning so that it doesn’t land on the erroneous configuration.

Shard the shared-expert weights to avoid redundant work. In order to do so we need to re-distribute the activations, which adds an extra AllGather and ReduceScatter.
This has been tested e2e to work and speed up decodes. So far, preliminary perf measurements show this is a decode win, and for prefill it’s a throughput vs kv cache size tradeoff.
FYI the performance and memory footprint improvements are overstated since all of the numbers are from running @mgoin’s 75% expert-sparse Kimi K3
Generated stuff below

Problem
Under sequence-parallel MoE, KimiMLP threads use_sequence_parallel straight through as disable_tp on both projections (model.py), so the dense and shared-expert MLPs are replicated on every rank. Each rank streams the entire weight to serve only its own token shard.
For Kimi-K3’s shared experts (hidden 7168, shared intermediate 6144):

gate_up  7168 x 12288 x 2B = 176.2 MB
down     6144 x  7168 x 2B =  88.1 MB
                           = 264.2 MB per layer per rank, replicated
x ~92 MoE layers           = ~22.6 GiB per rank

The routed experts are EP-sharded and the latent projections are deliberately replicated, but the shared experts are sharded by nothing — they sit outside the EP machinery, and disable_tp removes the only sharding they had.
This is visible from two independent directions:

Profiling. On a decode step the shared-expert GEMM pair is the second-largest line item after the MegaMoE routed GEMM. The kernels are healthy (~5.9 TB/s); the problem is byte count, not efficiency.
Memory budgets. A deployment spec whose weight budget assumed dense/TP + experts/(TP*DP) under-predicted actual per-GPU usage by ~28 GiB, of which the replicated shared experts account for ~23 GiB.

The replicated shapes have no entry, so under SP they fall through to cuBLAS — the table was tuned against the non-SP path, where these layers are TP-sharded.
Note this replicate-under-SP pattern is a vLLM-wide convention (DeepSeek-V4 does the same, with an explicit comment). Kimi-K3 is an outlier only because its shared expert is unusually large.
Change
Add VLLM_KIMI_K3_SHARD_SP_MLP (default off). Under the flag, KimiMLP TP-shards both projections and:

if self.shard_sequence_parallel:
  x = sp_all_gather(x)  # each rank owns disjoint tokens; gather the full set
gate_up, _ = self.gate_up_proj(x)
x = self.act_fn(gate_up)
x, _ = self.down_proj(x)  # RowParallel, partial over intermediate
if self.shard_sequence_parallel:
  x = sp_reduce_scatter(x)  # sums across TP and restores sequence sharding
The reduce-scatter does double duty, so the block still ends with one collective per direction rather than an all-reduce plus a re-shard.
Deliberately not enabled on the FusedMoE path, which hands the shared experts to the runner and assumes the replicated layout.
Trade-off and why it is opt-in
This trades weight bandwidth and resident memory for two collectives per layer. That only wins at low token counts, so it is off by default and intended for decode instances under P/D disaggregation, which can commit to the sharded layout and never see prefill-sized batches. Prefill instances should leave it off.
One known limitation: the flag is global, but prefill and decode want opposite answers. In a P/D deployment it can be scoped per role via the env var. In an aggregated deployment a single flag cannot be right for both — the dense MLP would shard on prefill, on the losing side of the crossover.

Purpose
Kimi-K3 checkpoints store e_score_correction_bias in FP32 and the AMD router already emits FP32 logits. The AMD model currently constructs the correction-bias parameter under the ambient BF16 model dtype, so the standard weight loader copies the FP32 checkpoint into BF16 storage. vllm-project/vllm#51274 · maeehart · MERGED · created 2026-08-06T15:09:53Z · merged 2026-10-03T06:28:02Z
Summary
Add an explicit int4_per_group_32 MoE override for Kimi-K3 on gfx942. When selected, the MXFP4 expert weights are requantized once at load time and served through AITER’s replacement BF16 x packed-int4 FlyDSL path.
The conversion is lossy and never happens by architecture alone. The default MXFP4 path is unchanged.
Why
gfx942 does not support the scaled FP4 conversion instructions used by the native MXFP4 path. This opt-in path pays the conversion cost once during model loading and then uses the replacement packed-int4 kernels from ROCm/aiter#4646.

Register int4_per_group_32 as a MoE weight quantization key.
Require the explicit --quantization-config.moe.weight int4_per_group_32 override on gfx942.
Require the replacement A16W4/int4 AITER entry point and fail closed unless it supports SiTUv2.
Convert eight experts at a time and release each source tensor before converting the next one, bounding transient memory during load.
Log a warning that the selected conversion is lossy.
Leave int4_per_group_32 out of the online MoE table so Mxfp4MoEMethod can convert at load time.

#51430 [Perf] Narrow DeepSeek V4 eager CUDA graph region
vllm-project/vllm#51430 · WoosukKwon · MERGED · created 2026-08-07T18:22:30Z · merged 2026-08-10T17:52:10Z
Summary
Narrow the DeepSeek V4 eager CUDA graph region so attention input preparation remains captured, and organize the flow so the execution stages are visible in one linear forward method.
The existing attention_impl eager break includes Q up-projection, fused Q normalization/RoPE/KV insertion, indexer input preparation, and MLA/indexer compression. This change moves those producer operations into forward and keeps only the sparse indexer operation plus forward_mqa in the eager region.
The final refactor removes the tuple-of-mostly-None plumbing, gives the input-projection helper a descriptive name and explicit return type, and reuses the indexer’s existing forward method. It adds no net methods.
This branch is synced with main at fac808b36f.
Parallelism
This does not reduce stream parallelism relative to main:

Input projections still use the default stream for fused_wqa_wkv plus three auxiliary streams for compressor KV score, indexer weights, and indexer compressor KV score.
The next stage still overlaps Q projection/KV insertion on the default stream with the indexer on auxiliary stream 0 and the MLA compressor on auxiliary stream 1.
Auxiliary stream 2 is reused by the indexer’s internal Q/K overlap.

The next stage still overlaps Q projection/KV insertion on the default stream with the indexer on auxiliary stream 0 and the MLA compressor on auxiliary stream 1.
Auxiliary stream 2 is reused by the indexer’s internal Q/K overlap.

ROCm retains its existing sequential fallback.
Why this approach
An earlier DeepSeek V4 region-narrowing change was reverted after real-model output corruption. This version deliberately keeps forward_mqa eager together with the sparse indexer instead of capturing the attention backend. Persistent eager scratch workspaces also keep the tensors consumed by the eager region address-stable.
This mirrors the region boundary used by the DeepSeek V3.2 optimization while preserving the DeepSeek V4 attention execution boundary.
Duplicate-work check
I searched open vLLM PRs for DeepSeek V4 CUDA graph, DeepSeek V4 eager attention, Narrow DeepSeek V4, and eager CUDA graph region DeepSeek. No other open PR implements this DeepSeek V4 eager-region narrowing. #51425 is the analogous DeepSeek V3.2 change and does not modify DeepSeek V4.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 4x GB200, Rust frontend, FP8 KV cache, FP4 indexer cache, PIECEWISE breakable CUDA graphs, DeepGEMM mega-MoE, and MTP2.

#51483 [Bugfix][Kimi-K3] Do not classify a stateless first chunk as a decode
vllm-project/vllm#51483 · sashko-zakharchuk · MERGED · created 2026-08-08T07:05:38Z · merged 2026-09-16T13:24:49Z
Purpose
Related to #51039.
A request being forwarded for the first time owns no KDA state, but the non-spec branch of the
Kimi-K3 KDA metadata builder classified any one-token row as a decode
(split_decodes_and_prefills(m, decode_threshold=1) with the default
treat_short_extends_as_decodes=True, nvidia/kda_metadata.py:405). When every row in a batch is one
token, num_prefills is 0, has_initial_state is never computed, and kda.py takes the
pure-decode route, which reads conv_state[slot] and recurrent_state[slot] unconditionally.
gather_initial_states is the only thing that masks a stateless slot, and it lives on the
prefill route. Mamba blocks are not zeroed on reallocation
(single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:86 restricts zero-on-allocate to the attention specs), so
such a request silently continues whatever KDA state the previous owner of its recycled block
left behind.
This builder already applies the correct rule on its spec path
(nvidia/kda_metadata.py:439-447, “Query length alone cannot distinguish a true decode from a
one-token prefill chunk”), and the Mamba2 builder does the same at mamba_attn.py:459-481
(“First-token prefills have no prior Mamba state and must stay prefills”).

Scheduler._mamba_block_aligned_split often clips that chunk to zero and drops the request from

Reachable on stock flags: a one-token prompt scheduled alongside ordinary decodes. Also
reachable when a request’s first chunk is clipped to one token by the remaining token budget
(scheduler.py:990). Under the default mamba_cache_mode="align",
Scheduler._mamba_block_aligned_split often clips that chunk to zero and drops the request from
the step instead. Two cases get through: a block-aligned chunk when the mamba spec carries
prefill checkpoint blocks and no Eagle drafter is configured, which is how Kimi-K3 runs under
the FlashKDA prefill backend (nvidia/kda.py:598), and any chunk when the mamba block size
exceeds the prefill budget (scheduler.py:419-436). A batch containing any row longer than one
token is unaffected, since nvidia/kda.py:824 then routes everything through the packed prefill
with the correct has_initial_state.
Three changes:

Classify by state rather than by query length. no_prior_state is computed from
seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound <= query_lens_cpu, which identifies rows with no computed tokens
(the bound is documented as precise for prefill rows and optimistic only for async spec
decode rows, backend.py:422-426; an optimistic bound can only miss a stateless row, never
promote a real decode), and it is additionally masked with the runner’s is_prefilling flag.
The dummy batch used for cudagraph capture also has seq_len == query_len for every row,
and without that mask the captured decode graph would record the prefill kernels.
One-token chunks that resume a partially prefilled request own valid state and keep the
decode path, so treat_short_extends_as_decodes=False alone would be wrong: it would move a
whole decode batch onto chunk_kda_with_fused_gate whenever a chunked prefill ends on a
one-token chunk.


Re-key the cudagraph staging guard. Decode-graph dispatch is shape based
(_is_uniform_decode decides from token counts before build() runs), so a one-token batch
can replay the captured decode graph even when a stateless first chunk makes it a prefill batch. Keyed on
num_prefills == 0 the guard would go false, staging would be skipped, and the replay would
read state indices staged in an earlier step. The new condition is the one the dispatcher
uses. On base this is a strict no-op: num_prefills == 0 and max_query_len <= 1 are
equivalent there, and the removed fill_(NULL_BLOCK_ID) is dead because entering the guard
implied num_decodes == batch_size (NULL padding still comes from the runner’s block table).

Exclude cudagraph padding from num_prefills. split_decodes_and_prefills returns
num_reqs - num_decodes, the whole suffix after the first prefill, so trailing zero-length
padding rows are counted as prefill requests once a stateless first chunk promotes a row ahead
of them. The value is only ever compared against zero downstream and never crosses zero, so no
routing decision changes. num_prefill_tokens is inflated separately, since it inherits
num_actual_tokens, which a full cudagraph pads past the last real token; it is recomputed
from the same real query boundary, and nothing on the KDA execution path reads it. The shared GDN
builder has all three defects, and #51565 makes the same changes there.

Note on blast radius: kda.py does not split the non-spec group, so once num_prefills > 0 the
whole non-spec batch takes the prefill route for that step. A single freshly admitted request
therefore moves an otherwise all-decode batch off ops.fused_kda_decode in eager, PIECEWISE,
and uncaptured sizes. Both prefill backends handle all-length-1 cu_seqlens correctly.
What this does not do. It corrects the metadata, not the dispatch. With the default
FULL_AND_PIECEWISE an all-one-token batch is still dispatched to the captured decode graph on
shape alone, so a replayed graph is unchanged; Mamba2 has the same residual gap. Closing it needs
either worker-side zeroing of mamba pages on reallocation or making the dispatcher decline the
full graph when a mamba group has a stateless row, both core-runner scope, and I am happy to
follow up on either.
It is also a no-op on batches whose metadata carries no is_prefilling flag, which is the
microbatching and context-parallel path (ubatch_utils._make_metadata_with_slice,
cp_utils.py): without the flag the builder cannot tell a first chunk from a resumed one-token
chunk, so it conservatively keeps the base classification there rather than promote a
capture-shaped batch by mistake.
On #51039 specifically: this is a correctness bug that needs no NaN, and it is also one way a
poisoned state block can be inherited by a brand-new request. It does not explain the origin of
the first NaN at 240K, so I am not claiming it resolves that incident.
Coordination: #50855 (draft) touches the same two files and adds an all_initial_states_fresh
flag computed from the same fresh-versus-resumed distinction this changes. Whoever lands second should re-check that flag against the new classification.
Line references above are against d9fbe526c, main at the time of writing.

This PR adds replace_as() — dataclasses.replace generalized to rebuild a spec as a different class — and drives the promotion from a source→target class mapping resolved through the MRO (the functools.singledispatch idiom, so subclasses hit their own entry first). Every shared field is carried automatically; new spec fields can no longer be silently lost in promotion.
Behavior changes (both bug fixes):

Promoted MLA and chunked-local specs now retain kv_quant_mode.
Promoted SlidingWindowMLASpec records its sliding_window, matching what the SlidingWindowSpec promotion already does per the FullAttentionSpec docstring (“we use FullAttentionSpec and record the sliding window size”).

#51855 [K3] support recoverssm for K3
vllm-project/vllm#51855 · ZJY0516 · MERGED · created 2026-08-11T17:49:54Z · merged 2026-08-17T11:34:14Z

Purpose
This PR adds RecoverSSM, a Kimi-K3-specific state recovery path for speculative KDA decoding on NVIDIA Model Runner V2. It is enabled through --use-replayssm, is intended for Kimi-K3 serving with DSpark, and supports mamba_cache_mode=align prefix caching.
Without RecoverSSM, KDA speculative decoding materializes a full recurrent state for every speculative position. RecoverSSM keeps one checkpoint and compact per-token records, then reconstructs the state at the accepted position after every verify. Under the tested TP8 Kimi-K3 configuration, this increases the effective cache capacity by 10.97% at the same 46.48 GiB cache-memory budget.
Design
Kimi-K3-specific MRV2 integration
The implementation is contained in the Kimi-K3 KDA metadata, layer, and RecoverSSM operator paths. The metadata builder gives speculative rows one KDA checkpoint slot and creates a model-specific post-sampling committer.
RecoverSSM is selected through the existing --use-replayssm option. The regular KDA prefill and non-speculative decode paths are unchanged.
Verify records FP32 corrections
KDA verify reads the checkpoint without modifying it and computes the normal speculative outputs. For each speculative token it records:

the correction vector u in FP32;
the key and raw gate in the activation dtype.

Recording u removes v and beta from the commit path and avoids recomputing the state-dependent correction. FP32 is used for u to preserve reconstruction accuracy; keys and gates remain BF16 in the evaluated configuration.
Direct accepted-position reconstruction
After verification determines the accepted length, one Triton kernel reconstructs the required checkpoint directly. For the KDA recurrence:

S_t = S_{t-1} * exp(g_t) + u_t outer k_t
The accepted state is:

the correction vector u in FP32;
the key and raw gate in the activation dtype.

Recording u removes v and beta from the commit path and avoids recomputing the state-dependent correction. FP32 is used for u to preserve reconstruction accuracy; keys and gates remain BF16 in the evaluated configuration.
Direct accepted-position reconstruction
After verification determines the accepted length, one Triton kernel reconstructs the required checkpoint directly. For the KDA recurrence:

S_t = S_{t-1} * exp(g_t) + u_t outer k_t
The accepted state is:

S_p = S_0 * exp(sum(g_1 ... g_p))
    + sum_j u_j outer (k_j * exp(sum(g_{j+1} ... g_p)))
The commit kernel evaluates this expression in reverse token order. It loads the original state once and does not recursively update or write intermediate states. The loop bound is the runtime accepted length rather than the complete eight-token DSpark activation window.
In align mode, the same launch also reconstructs the next prefix-cache boundary when the accepted range crosses it. Convolution history is compacted to the accepted position and to the boundary using the same commit plan.
Cache layout
Each KDA page contains:

(convolution state, KDA checkpoint, FP32 correction records, key/gate records)
Recovery records are transient and are not included in prefix-cache state copies. The checkpoint and convolution state remain the prefix-cache boundary state.
Scope

NVIDIA Kimi-K3 KDA
Model Runner V2
speculative decoding, validated with Kimi-K3-DSpark and seven draft tokens
mamba_cache_mode=align prefix caching

Shared changes are limited to the derived KDA RecoverSSM flag, state-layout helpers, and the post-sampling commit lifecycle. The recovery algorithm and cache layout remain Kimi-K3-specific, and this PR does not add Mamba2 support.

gates with and without a lower bound;
cache shape and dtype derivation.

Summary
This PR adds FlashInfer as an optional ReplaySSM backend for Mamba2. It calls FlashInfer’s native checkpointing_ssu API, shares replay trackers per KV-cache group, and autotunes a maximum-batch decode through the existing FlashInfer warmup flow before CUDA-graph capture. FlashInfer ReplaySSM supports Model Runner V1 and V2; Triton ReplaySSM remains V1-only.

Hi @wangyicong52, I tested the current head 3d52c83 and found two issues:


The new validation bypass allows Hybrid requests to reach an incorrect GDN slicing path.
For example, with Hkv=4, P TP4 -> D TP8, the base version rejects the request because the Attention region lengths do not satisfy the TP ratio. This PR skips that check when the consumer is replicated, allowing the GDN group to be transferred as well.
Here, is_mamba_group=True only bypasses the new head mapping; the planner still slices the entire Mamba page according to the TP ratio:
github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d52c8329ded27d62e043c960cc3e2250a5c02de/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py#L2081-L2086
However, the conv and SSM states within the page need to be sharded separately. Taking the first or second half of the entire page does not produce the correct destination state. In the H20 test, the Attention contents were correct, but all 3,840 conv elements on D rank 1 were incorrect, while the sender still returned FINISH + ok_reqs.
Reproduction script

Skipping length validation for a replicated consumer can report success after writing only part of the destination region.
This condition bypasses region-length validation entirely:
github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d52c8329ded27d62e043c960cc3e2250a5c02de/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py#L267-L268
For Hkv=4, TP1 -> TP8, if the P region is 256 KiB, or 64 KiB per head, while D advertises a 128 KiB region for its single head, validation currently passes. The planner copies only 64 KiB. The subsequent assertions also pass because they only check whether the copy exceeds either region:
github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d52c8329ded27d62e043c960cc3e2250a5c02de/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py#L1563-L1568
The other half of D’s region remains unwritten, but the request is still reported as successful.
Reproduction script

#52816 [Spec Decode] DFlash2: local convolution + candidate selector
vllm-project/vllm#52816 · SubSir · MERGED · created 2026-08-18T19:28:50Z · merged 2026-08-21T05:27:22Z
Two additions to the DFlash drafter, carried by a separate architecture:
a checkpoint declaring DFlash2DraftModel gets them, and every existing
DFlashDraftModel checkpoint resolves to the class it resolves to today,
untouched by this PR.
Grouped dynamic depthwise convolution inside each block, so a proposal
position can see the ones before it without another backbone pass.
out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c], taps zero across the block
boundary. Wraps each sublayer in and out from one projection of its input.
Sized by conv_kernel_size and conv_group_size in the draft config.
Candidate selector. Instead of an independent argmax per slot, keep the
target head’s top-K per slot, score adjacent transitions
edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c], and walk the best path from
the verified anchor. At T>0 it walks by inverse CDF and returns q over the K
candidates for the lossless verify. Sized by selector_rank and
selector_top_k in the draft config.

model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py            the convolution and the selector
v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash2/speculator.py   the walk kernel and the proposal
model_executor/models/registry.py                 DFlash2DraftModel
v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/__init__.py             speculator selection

model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py            the convolution and the selector
v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash2/speculator.py   the walk kernel and the proposal
model_executor/models/registry.py                 DFlash2DraftModel
v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/__init__.py             speculator selection

The selector runs after the draft model’s forward and carries its own
@support_torch_compile. The path walk is one Triton program per request: a
slot’s K scores stay in registers, and the slot-to-slot dependency is a loop
inside the program rather than a kernel per slot. The vocabulary top-k, the
selector’s largest single cost, uses FlashInfer’s radix kernel where FlashInfer
is available and torch.topk otherwise.
DFlash2 runs on the V2 model runner, which is where its speculator lives.
use_v2_model_runner selects V2 for a DFlash2 draft, as it already does for
DSpark: the V1 DFlashProposer has no candidate selector, so a DFlash2
checkpoint reaching it would draft as DFlash1 without raising.
Results
Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B on one H200, against
RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark
and autoregressive decoding. Seven draft tokens per verification step for both
drafters. Qwen3.8’s recommended sampling — temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20
— with xhigh reasoning effort and 4096 max new tokens; prompt formatting from
z-lab/dflash.
Acceptance length, GSM8K
Mean over per-request acceptance, the statistic the model cards report. vLLM’s
counters give a pooled ratio — total accepted tokens over total drafts — so the
per-request values are recovered at concurrency 1, where a counter delta around
a single request belongs to that request alone.

DSparkDFlash 2per-request mean4.275.34+25.2%pooled ratio3.644.65+27.8%
Acceptance does not move with concurrency: DFlash 2’s pooled ratio reads 4.65,
4.82 and 4.74 at concurrency 1, 8 and 32.
Throughput, GSM8K
Output tokens over end-to-end wall time. Each point is 128 × concurrency
requests split over four shards, each shard one H200 serving at the stated
concurrency; the four shard rates are averaged, not summed, so a cell is a
single-GPU number measured four times. A warmup of concurrency requests runs
before the clock starts and is dropped, as in z-lab/dflash.

All three methods are served one after another inside the same container, so a

Each component timed alone in its own CUDA graph at the shapes the draft runs

The selector’s own math — the lattice and the walk — is 0.020 ms and flat in
batch; the rest of that column is the vocabulary top-k, where FlashInfer’s radix
kernel is 1.9× torch.topk at batch 1 and 4.5× at batch 32.
The convolution is 20 small calls over [8, 5120] tensors, so it is
launch-bound rather than FLOP-bound: 0.477 ms as eager modules, 0.0096 ms
compiled as a single graph across all 20 calls, and 0.113 ms — the figure above
— with each call compiled on its own, which is what the model’s compiled region
gives it, since attention and the MLP run between prepare and finish. A
hand-fused kernel would collect most of the remaining 12×.

I found a CandidateSelector compile-cache namespace collision while testing this PR with:

target: unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
drafter: incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
num_speculative_tokens: 7
hardware: DGX Spark (SM121)
Note: reaching this path with the Unsloth target required a separate local change to relax DFlash2’s unquantized-lm_head restriction. I’ll post the quantized FP8 lm_head results separately on #52883.
With that change, the existing quant_method.apply() candidate path worked, but startup failed in CandidateSelector.
CandidateSelector has its own @support_torch_compile, but is constructed while the active model_tag is dflash_head. In this configuration its VllmBackend shared the parent DFlash2 compile-cache namespace.
On a clean compile cache:

dflash_head:
  Compiling a graph for compile range (1, 12288)
 
CandidateSelector:
  Directly load the compiled graph(s) for compile range (1, 12288) from the cache
  ...
  ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 12, got 8)
Just clearing the persistent cache did not help. The wrong graph was reused within the same startup.
Giving the selector its own namespace fixes it:

from vllm.compilation.backends import set_model_tag
 
with set_model_tag('dflash2_candidate_selector'):
  self.candidate_selector = CandidateSelector(
    hidden_size=self.config.hidden_size,
    vocab_size=self.config.vocab_size,
    rank=int(draft_config['selector_rank']),
    top_k=int(draft_config['selector_top_k']),
    params_dtype=vllm_config.model_config.dtype,
    prefix=maybe_prefix(prefix, 'candidate_selector'),
  )
Afterward it compiles separately:

.../rank_0_0/dflash2_candidate_selector
Compiling a graph for compile range (1, 12288) takes 0.89 s
and DFlash2 completes profiling, KV-cache initialization, CUDA graph capture, and server startup.
I ran tool-eval-bench to validate the fix. In this configuration DFlash2 outperformed the MTP drafter baseline with comparable accuracy, and the server processed 1,064 requests without request errors, aborts, or preemptions.
This appears to be a compile-cache namespace collision: the selector is loading a compiled artifact with a different input signature (12 vs 8), rather than an Inductor signature-generation issue.
This is separate from the sampling/probabilistic-correctness and runtime OOB issues already being discussed on this PR.

Two things have to be true at the same time: the AOT split schedule is on, and there are enough splits that the combine kernel runs at all. Turning off either one stops it in every run we tried.
A workaround you can use now: drop —attention-backend flashinfer. We tested it, 3/3 clean with everything else the same as your config. The reason is that _get_sliding_window_configs only counts FlashAttention layers. With the target on FlashInfer the builder only sees the draft’s layers, they all have the same window, so the AOT schedule stays on. With the target on FlashAttention it sees two different windows and drops the schedule by itself. SGLang does the same thing on purpose for sliding-window layers.
This isn’t a real fix and it does change your target’s backend, so it’s just to unblock you for now.

incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2, TP=8, num_speculative_tokens=7. It works —
187–207 tok/s on a coding workload, mean acceptance length 4.47/8, against
66.8 tok/s for the same model with no speculation. Roughly 3x.
Getting there took a dozen boots across four configurations, and two of the failures look like they may be the
same underlying issue as three of the open reports on this PR. Sharing the matrix
in case it is useful.
What we hit, and what fixed it

























cudagraph configurationresultFULL_AND_PIECEWISE (default)Memory access fault, all 8 GPUs. Fires on the first request, or during warmup_kernels if anything perturbs timingpiecewise graph containing attention (VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1)Starts, runs, mean acceptance length 1.00 — every draft rejected, silently--enforce-eagercorrect, acceptance 4–5, but slow (53–75 tok/s)piecewise with attention split outcorrect and fast: 4.47 acceptance, 187–207 tok/s
The middle two rows are the interesting ones: the same underlying condition
produced a hard fault in one configuration and silent garbage in another.
Why we think it may be one bug, not two
The faulting configuration captures the drafter’s graph; the silent-garbage
configuration captures the target’s forward with attention inside the graph.
In both, the evidence points to a captured graph replayed against state it was not captured for (mechanism confirmed for the silent-garbage row; inferred from the fault location for the fault row).
What differs is only what happens when the replay reads memory it should not:

PyTorch’s caching allocator does not return freed blocks to the driver, so
on CUDA the address usually stays mapped — the replay reads stale data and you
get wrong output, not a crash.
On ROCm the same access can land on a page that is no longer mapped, and ROCr’s
handler aborts the process with Memory access fault by GPU node-N.

This is a hypothesis, not something we verified — we have no CUDA hardware to
test the other half. But if it holds, then:

@benchislett’s garbage output (!!!!!!) and NaNs,
@timothysu’s vectorized_gather_kernel: index out of bounds under concurrency,
@ChengYen-Tang’s failure “after running for a while”,
and our hard faults

are the same defect observed through two different allocator behaviours, and
fixing the value-level symptoms alone would leave the address-level cause in place.
Compatibility notes for this PR

ROCm/CDNA3 works. @2imi9 reported success on MI308X with triton 3.6; we are
on triton 3.7.1 / torch 2.12 and also fine, so the triton version does not
appear to be a factor.
The USE_FP64 fp32/fp64 branch-type fix already in this PR
(.to(tl.float64 if USE_FP64 else tl.float32)) was required for us as well.
#52883’s unquantized-LM-head fix is already absorbed here
(accept an unquantized linear LM head as well); our bf16 target needs the
UnquantizedEmbeddingMethod branch and it works.
Our drafter attention backend resolved to ROCM_ATTN
(ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN was rejected as incompatible).

Configuration we ended up with
Speculative decoding here is only correct when attention is outside the
piecewise graph. Any configuration that puts attention back inside it
(we hit it via VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1, which skips the empty-splitting-ops
guard; other routes that empty splitting_ops appear to carry their own
cudagraph-mode downgrades) reintroduces the silent-rejection failure, because piecewise
graph entries are keyed by BatchDescriptor, which does not encode the
per-request query length — so a 2x8 verify batch and a 16x1 decode batch share a
key. Filed separately as vllm-project/vllm#53030; mentioning it here because it is what makes the
“acceptance 1.00” row above reproducible.
Happy to re-run anything on this hardware.

39.1  NVFP4     head   0.64 GB

37.8  FP8 stored at BF16 width, 2.54 GB
37.5  BF16      head   2.54 GB
...
34.7  BF16      head   2.54 GB

The mechanism is straightforward: under speculation the head runs once per draft position while the body runs once per step, so head bytes dominate decode. Guarding against quantized heads excludes exactly the configurations that benefit most.
RadixArk above is the most aggressive case — NVFP4 weights and 4-bit activations — and it is also the lowest TTFT measured here at 4.5 s, accept length 4.32. Nothing is dequantized; the head stays packed. The call already goes through quant_method.apply(), and the padding and TP handling below it are scheme-agnostic.

e-d-y-o-s (2026-08-20T10:55:55Z):
Field report from a single RTX 5090 (32GB), in case it saves someone the two days it cost us. We cherry-picked this PR onto our production fork (base + a few local patches), all 19 PR tests pass without a GPU, and ran it against Muse-Glimmer-30B in NVFP4 with the incoai DFlash2 drafter.
The good news first, because it is genuinely good:

The port is clean. Two trivial conflicts (registry comment, a context-only test), everything else applies as-is.
Acceptance delivers what the paper promises: 1.19 tokens accepted per draft at nst=2 greedy (pos0 71%, pos1 48%), against 0.92 for the v1 drafter on the same card. At our production sampling (T=0.1, top_p 0.95, min_p 0.03) it holds at 0.93-0.94.
Throughput with distinct prompts (no shared prefixes — our first sweep had them and it distorted everything): +25% at 8 concurrent, +17% at 32, +15% at 64, on top of a no-spec baseline at 1.8k tok/s. nst=2 beats nst=15 everywhere on this card; the README default of 15 wastes 85% of its verification slots here.
We quantized the drafter to W4A16 (data-free RTN, int4 g128, decoder MLP projections only) because no 4-bit DFlash2 drafter exists on the hub. Acceptance is unchanged versus bf16 — the quantization is free on this metric. One sharp edge: only quantize the MLP. We tried adding fc and o_proj and the engine dies at load with 'QKVParallelLinear' object has no attribute 'data' — the DFlash context-KV precompute reads qkv_proj.weight as a dense tensor, and an ignore-list written against HF names (q_proj/k_proj/v_proj) does not protect the fused qkv_proj the loader actually asks about.

The bad news is the VRAM arithmetic on 32GB, and it is unforgiving:

The bad news is the VRAM arithmetic on 32GB, and it is unforgiving:

The bf16 drafter is 5.16 GiB of weights (lm_head and embeddings are shared with the target — good design, they cost nothing). With a multimodal target (vision tower resident) there is simply no room left for a usable KV pool.
Even with the 2.4 GiB quantized drafter, the best stable config we found caps the KV pool at about 40% of what the same server allocates without speculation. We swept gpu-memory-utilization and cudagraph sizes; above that point we hit a constant OOM wall during graph capture regardless of how much KV we gave back.
And the drafter’s KV has a shape worth knowing: five full-width layers with a 2048 sliding window is a near-fixed per-request cost, so it is proportionally most expensive exactly where production lives — at 8-16k contexts it adds 34-39% KV per request, while at 131k it only adds 10%. The engine’s “GPU KV cache size: N tokens” line is anchored to max_model_len, which makes the hit look much smaller than it is for short-context workloads.

So on this card the trade is +15-26% throughput against roughly half the resident concurrency at realistic context lengths, and we ended up not deploying it — the speedup is real but the concurrency is what pays our bills. On 48GB+ none of this should bind and the PR looks like a straight win. Two things would change the picture on consumer hardware: an official quantized drafter (our RTN numbers suggest it is free quality-wise), and possibly a knob to cap the drafter’s KV admission separately from the target’s.
Happy to share the quantization recipe or the sweep harness if useful.

#52928 [Mamba] Add FlashInfer ReplaySSM support for MTP
vllm-project/vllm#52928 · askliar · MERGED · created 2026-08-19T10:37:28Z · merged 2026-09-30T21:41:18Z
Summary
This stacked follow-up extends the native FlashInfer ReplaySSM integration from single-token decode in #52506 to multi-token prediction (MTP) verification for Mamba2 models.
With MTP, the model evaluates one target token plus several draft tokens before sampling determines how many were accepted. ReplaySSM avoids materializing a separate recurrent state for every speculative token: each layer keeps a checkpoint and a ring of inputs, the accepted length advances a shared cursor before the next forward, and the checkpoint is updated only when the next verification window would overflow the ring.

The FlashInfer path also depends on the compatible ReplaySSM API and native autotuning work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4545.
Design

IMPORTANT 



This PR is stacked on #52506 and must not merge independently. Until #52506 lands, GitHub shows the cumulative base and MTP changes in this diff.


The FlashInfer path also depends on the compatible ReplaySSM API and native autotuning work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4545.
Design

MTP-shaped execution: uniform verification batches use dense (batch, tokens, ...) inputs so FlashInfer can select its native MTP tactics. Variable-length batches use the packed cu_seqlens interface.
One acceptance update per cache group: every Mamba layer observes the same accepted-token count, so ring cursors are shared and advanced once per model forward. Checkpoints and ring payloads remain layer-local.
One state page per request: ReplaySSM stores one physical Mamba state page rather than one page per target/draft position. The causal-conv1d verification length is passed separately from the physical block-table width.
CUDA-graph-safe indexing: the contiguous FlashInfer state-index vector lives in persistent runner-owned storage and is refreshed before replay, keeping its captured address stable.
Native FlashInfer selection: the ReplaySSM call uses FlashInfer’s checkpointing_ssu API and native autotuning. PDL is forwarded explicitly but defaults off because it was not a consistent end-to-end win.
No duplicate Triton implementation: #49847 implements MTP ReplaySSM using separate Triton kernels, a token-major ring, and its own cursor lifecycle. This PR retains the FlashInfer layout and delegates the update to native FlashInfer instead of copying the Triton kernel stack into vLLM.

This PR does not modify FlashInfer or add prefix-cache alignment support. ReplaySSM continues to use mamba_cache_mode=none.

Production-profile findings
Nsight Systems profiles used 64 steady CUDA-graph decode steps and summed ReplaySSM work over all 23 Mamba layers:

H100 caseFlashInfer kernelsTriton kernelsFlashInfer trackerTriton trackerB16, AL4739.42 μs/step644.74 μs/step6.89 μs/step10.87 μs/stepB128, AL43,529.11 μs/step3,587.91 μs/step8.50 μs/step12.69 μs/step
The eager microbenchmark showed a much larger FlashInfer advantage because the Triton path issued several kernels from Python. CUDA-graph replay removes most of that dispatch and inter-launch gap. In production graphs, B16 favors the Triton kernels while B128 is effectively tied; the shared FlashInfer tracker is consistently cheaper.
On GB200 at B256, ReplaySSM accounted for approximately 16% of execute-step GPU time. Its 1.56× in-model improvement predicts a maximum whole-step gain of roughly 6.1%, close to the measured 5.65%. This explains why a much larger isolated-kernel ratio becomes a mid-single-digit end-to-end improvement.

vllm-project/vllm#52988 · qiching · MERGED · created 2026-08-19T18:00:52Z · merged 2026-09-23T03:43:33Z
Summary
Make Kimi-K3’s MLA and KDA decode paths capturable as FULL varlen CUDA graphs so they work under adaptive DSpark verification (#47808), which schedules ragged per-request draft budgets and requires device-sourced query lengths. Before this change K3’s FLASHINFER_MLA reported UNIFORM_BATCH/UNIFORM, and the decode builders derived per-request query length from a measured/averaged count, so a graph captured on a uniform dummy did not match ragged replay.
Changes
FlashInfer MLA (flashinfer_mla.py)

Promote _cudagraph_support to AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS and query_len_support to QueryLenSupport.VARLEN.
On the causal spec-decode path, pass cum_seq_lens_q + max_q_len to trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla (flashinfer #3238); assert this path runs on trtllm-gen and does not return LSE (mutually exclusive with DCP).
Flatten non-causal and DCP decode rows by mapping each row to its request with searchsorted on the device query offsets instead of repeat_interleave(uniform_len).
Carry query_start_loc_device, cum_seq_lens_q, and max_query_len on the decode metadata; set cum_seq_lens_q only when max_query_len > 1.

MLA common (mla_attention.py + subclass builders)

Thread a promised max_query_len through MLACommonMetadataBuilder._build_decode (clamped to reorder_batch_threshold) and the flashmla, flashattn_mla, rocm_aiter_mla, and dots3_note builders.

KDA (kda_metadata.py)

Promote KimiK3KDAMetadataBuilder to AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS.
Route every active decode through the spec path by masking on is_prefilling rather than draft count.
Return True from supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch.

KDA RecoverSSM (kda_metadata.py, opt-in via --use-replayssm, off by default)

Make RecoverSSM co-exist with the adaptive path so it can drop the KDA spec-decode SSM state from num_spec+1 slots to 1 per request (kernels already in #51855):

Build the confidence head when the config enables it, load its weights (skipped only when the draft did not build one), and expose compute_confidence.

#53129 [KV Connector] Support heterogeneous TP sharing in Mooncake Store Connector
vllm-project/vllm#53129 · z-zanez · MERGED · created 2026-08-20T15:51:57Z · merged 2026-09-01T17:18:07Z
Purpose
This PR allows vLLM instances using the same backend-native LBHNC or LBNHC
layout, whose TP sizes divide a common Store TP size, to share the same KV
cache through Mooncake Store. Sharing vLLM instances must use the same PP size
and satisfy the KV-head and topology requirements described below.
Previously, Mooncake Store keys and physical data layouts were tied to the
local TP rank. Even when Prefill and Decode instances used the same model,
different TP sizes produced different Store shard counts, KV-head ranges, and
key namespaces, so the instances could not hit the same KV cache entries.
This PR introduces a fixed Store TP layout that decouples Store objects from
the local TP size of a vLLM instance:

store_tp_size defines a stable number of logical Store shards;
for regular MHA/GQA sharing, each Store shard contains a fixed range of
global KV heads;
one local TP rank maps to one or more consecutive Store shards;
vLLM instances with different local TP sizes can read and write the same key
namespace when they use the same native KV layout and Store TP size;
a Decode consumer with save_decode_cache enabled writes newly completed
decode KV blocks back in the same Store TP layout.

The implementation separates logical token enumeration from the Store payload
layout:

ChunkedTokenDatabase enumerates logical token chunks and their hashes;
StoreLayout defines Store keys, required lookup shards, local buffer spans,
and KV-cache tensor registration and validation;
the transfer workers execute layout-provided Store operations without
model- or layout-specific branches.

RankLocalStoreLayout preserves the existing rank-local format, while
LBHNCStoreLayout and LBNHCStoreLayout implement the common Store TP shard
formats used by this PR.
For example, with Store TP size 4:

each TP4 rank maps to one Store shard;
each TP2 rank maps to two Store shards;
KV written by a TP4 Prefill instance can be read by a TP2 Decode instance;
KV written back by the TP2 Decode instance can be reused by compatible TP4
or TP2 instances.

RankLocalStoreLayout preserves the existing rank-local format, while
LBHNCStoreLayout and LBNHCStoreLayout implement the common Store TP shard
formats used by this PR.
For example, with Store TP size 4:

each TP4 rank maps to one Store shard;
each TP2 rank maps to two Store shards;
KV written by a TP4 Prefill instance can be read by a TP2 Decode instance;
KV written back by the TP2 Decode instance can be reused by compatible TP4
or TP2 instances.

The Store layout follows the attention backend’s resolved LBHNC
([layers, blocks, KV heads, tokens, head size]) or LBNHC
([layers, blocks, tokens, KV heads, head size]) layout. LBHNC uses contiguous
head ranges directly. LBNHC represents each shard as token-wise head ranges
through Mooncake multi-buffer I/O. Neither path changes the attention
backend’s selected layout or requires a layout-conversion staging buffer.
Because the layout is encoded in the Store namespace, LBHNC and LBNHC
endpoints use separate Store entries rather than reading each other’s payloads.
Deployments with multiple Prefill TP sizes can explicitly select a common
Store TP size:

{ "kv_connector_extra_config": { "enable_store_tp_lcm": true, "prefill_tp_sizes": [4, 2] } }
When enable_store_tp_lcm is enabled, the connector uses the least common
multiple of prefill_tp_sizes as the common Store TP size. For example, the
least common multiple of 4 and 2 is 4, so the configuration above selects
Store TP size 4. This selection does not change the runtime TP size of any
vLLM instance.
All Prefill and Decode instances sharing the namespace calculate the same
Store TP size from the same configuration. Decode does not inspect which
Prefill TP size produced an individual request and does not change its write
layout per request. With Prefill TP sizes 4 and 2 and Decode TP size 2, all
using the same supported KV layout:

each TP4 Prefill rank writes one Store shard;
each TP2 Prefill rank writes two Store shards;
each TP2 Decode rank reads and writes two Store shards.

each TP4 Prefill rank writes one Store shard;
each TP2 Prefill rank writes two Store shards;
each TP2 Decode rank reads and writes two Store shards.

Decode therefore writes according to the common Store TP size, rather than its
own local TP size or the TP size of a particular Prefill instance. Its local KV
heads are mapped back to the same global Store shards, so decode KV written by
one compatible topology remains reusable by the others.
When automatic common Store TP size selection is not enabled, all vLLM
instances use the explicitly configured store_tp_size and follow the same
mapping rules.
The vLLM instances must already satisfy the existing Mooncake Store
compatibility requirements (same model/KV format, block and hash
configuration, and cache namespace). Heterogeneous-TP sharing additionally
requires:

all sharing endpoints use the same LBHNC or LBNHC KV cache layout;
Store TP size is greater than or equal to local TP size;
Store TP size is divisible by local TP size;
for MHA/GQA, the model’s total number of KV heads is divisible by Store TP
size; MQA (Hkv == 1) uses a replicated shared layout instead;
all sharing vLLM instances use the same PP size;
the KV cache contains one Full Attention group;
PCP and DCP are not used.

Different local TP sizes give each rank a different number of KV heads. This
implementation first divides the model’s global KV heads into fixed Store
shards and then maps each local rank’s KV heads to one or more consecutive
Store shards. MQA is handled separately: because every TP rank holds the same
single KV head, it uses a replicated shared layout instead of regular
Store-head partitioning.
vLLM instances with different PP sizes do not share a Store namespace. The PP
size is encoded in the namespace, preventing incompatible PP topologies from
hitting each other’s KV cache entries. The KV layout is also encoded, so
LBHNC and LBNHC instances remain isolated from each other.
If any sharing condition is not satisfied, the connector falls back to an
isolated rank-local namespace that includes the local TP, PP, and KV layout.
This PR also updates the Mooncake Store Connector documentation and adds
regression coverage for:

LBHNC and LBNHC Store-shard mapping and round trips across different TP
sizes;
vLLM instances whose ranks hold different numbers of KV heads;
layout-specific shared Store key namespaces;
common Store TP size selection for multiple Prefill TP sizes;
PP namespace isolation;
rank-local fallback for unsupported layouts, malformed configurations, and
incompatible topologies;
the shared MQA namespace;
logical-block KV event aggregation for multi-shard Store writes, including
partial shard failures and mixed existing/missing shards;
replication-aware KV event aggregation for GQA and MQA TP striping.

Related Issues and PRs

Issue #45036 tracks the Mooncake Store Connector roadmap and lists
“Decode-Phase KV Cache Put with GQA TP Asymmetry” as an open item. This PR
covers the Full Attention case where TP sizes are divisible, PP sizes match,
and KV heads can be partitioned by a common Store TP size.
PR #36869 added heterogeneous-TP support to MooncakeConnector for direct
P/D KV transfer. In contrast, this PR targets MooncakeStoreConnector, where
KV is persisted using a stable Store-shard layout and can be reused and
updated by multiple Prefill and Decode instances.

extends that path so Prefill and Decode instances with different TP sizes can
read and write the same KV cache using a common Store TP size.

exceeds the number of KV heads and the heads are replicated. This PR uses a
separate Store-shard mapping and limits regular sharing to topologies where
the total number of KV heads is divisible by Store TP size. Unsupported
topologies fall back to an isolated rank-local namespace.

#53396 [Kimi K3][Kernel] Support DS conv-state layout in fused KDA decode kernel
vllm-project/vllm#53396 · gcanlin · MERGED · created 2026-08-22T19:17:12Z · merged 2026-08-27T06:54:51Z
Summary
The fused KDA decode kernel (ops.fused_kda_decode) previously required the SD conv-state cache layout, so any deployment that pins VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS — required for NIXL point-to-point state transfer in P/D-disaggregated serving — silently bypassed the fused path and fell back to the multi-op Triton decode chain for all 69 KDA layers of the model.
This PR supports both physical cache layouts by dispatching to separate SD- and DS-specialized fused-kernel instantiations. Keeping each layout’s address calculation compile-time constant avoids the extra integer instructions and register pressure caused by runtime inner strides. Both layouts now use the fused path (in-proj GEMM → fused KDA decode → out-proj GEMM per layer and step), and numerics are bit-identical for identical inputs.
Update (head 0e67480f): per review feedback, the layout specialization is now expressed as two integer conv-state inner strides (channel, tap) as non-type template parameters instead of a layout enum. The generated device code is unchanged — see the parity data below.
Motivation

Deployment reality: production K3 serving pins VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS (NIXL PD transfer), and several recent fixes treat DS as the supported production layout. Under DS, the fused kernel was never used.
Measured cost of the fallback chain on B200 (TP8 shape, H_local=12, K=V=128): 1.16-1.58x slower than the fused kernel depending on batch, plus ~3x launch count in the per-layer decode chain (8-9 vs 3 kernels).

#53614 [Kimi K3] Support internal prefix checkpoints with partial prefix caching and spec-decoding
vllm-project/vllm#53614 · ZeldaHuang · MERGED · created 2026-08-24T18:26:18Z · merged 2026-09-06T05:18:16Z
Purpose
Extend the Kimi-K3 prefill checkpoint optimization from #52789 to support:

speculative decoding / Eagle block rewind;
partial prefix caching (prefix_match_unit < Mamba block size); and
checkpoint blocks restored through KV connectors such as MooncakeStore.

The cache manager and FlashKDA worker share the same checkpoint-validity rules, so a checkpoint block is allocated and hashed only when the worker can write it. For an aligned partial checkpoint, the already reserved request-owned checkpoint block is re-keyed from its provisional boundary to the state position actually exported by FlashKDA.
This PR keeps the block allocation, eviction, and free lifecycle introduced in #52789.

#53781 [3/N] HiSparse: host-resident sparse-MLA decode hot-buffering
vllm-project/vllm#53781 · MatthewBonanni · MERGED · created 2026-08-25T19:21:03Z · merged 2026-09-12T04:36:47Z
Summary
HiSparse adds a host-resident tier beneath vLLM’s normal GPU KV cache for sparse-MLA decode. Unlike the original always-host-resident design in #46326, this implementation keeps as much KV as possible in the normal device cache and spills pages to pinned host memory only when GPU capacity must be reclaimed.
Supersedes #46326.
Design overview

resident GPU pages
        |
        | spill under pressure
        v
  pinned host pool ---- selected top-k misses ----> per-request GPU hot buffer
        ^                                                     |
        |                                                     v
        +---------------- prefix reuse ---------------- sparse attention
The active indexer cache remains device-resident and produces the logical top-k positions needed by sparse attention. A fused CUDA resolver maps each selected position through three possible locations:

a normal resident GPU page;
an existing row in the request’s GPU hot buffer;
the pinned host pool.

resident GPU pages
        |
        | spill under pressure
        v
  pinned host pool ---- selected top-k misses ----> per-request GPU hot buffer
        ^                                                     |
        |                                                     v
        +---------------- prefix reuse ---------------- sparse attention
The active indexer cache remains device-resident and produces the logical top-k positions needed by sparse attention. A fused CUDA resolver maps each selected position through three possible locations:

a normal resident GPU page;
an existing row in the request’s GPU hot buffer;
the pinned host pool.

Resident hits return before the hot-cache lookup. Hot hits update a GPU-side LRU, while misses replace LRU entries by gathering only the selected host rows. Resolution, replacement, and LRU updates remain on the GPU and are compatible with CUDA graph replay.
HiSparse does not maintain a private host-side copy of indexer KV. The indexer remains a normal prefix-cacheable GPU cache group. When OffloadingConnector is configured alongside HiSparse, generic KV offloading preserves and restores the indexer while HiSparse continues to own only sparse-MLA residency. If the sparse host prefix extends beyond the available indexer prefix, the scheduler restores only the missing indexer suffix, capped at the sparse host boundary. Without generic offloading, the request falls back to the shorter shared prefix and recomputes the remainder.
Residency and ownership
The normal KV cache manager continues to own GPU block allocation. HiSparseCoordinator owns logical host blocks, host-prefix identity, and residency transitions.
When GPU pressure requires reclaiming a resident page, the coordinator reserves its host destination and sends a transfer command to the worker. The resident GPU block becomes reusable after every worker has acknowledged that the copy is enqueued in stream order. The host page is not published for prefix reuse until every copy has completed.
The main components are:

HiSparseCoordinator: scheduler-side host allocation, prefix state, and spill policy.
HiSparseConnector: carries residency commands and transfer acknowledgements between scheduler and workers.
HiSparseConnectorWorker: manages the pinned host-pool lifecycle and executes copies.
HiSparseRuntime: owns each cache’s host/hot views, GPU LRU state, and fused attention-time resolution.

HiSparseCoordinator: scheduler-side host allocation, prefix state, and spill policy.
HiSparseConnector: carries residency commands and transfer acknowledgements between scheduler and workers.
HiSparseConnectorWorker: manages the pinned host-pool lifecycle and executes copies.
HiSparseRuntime: owns each cache’s host/hot views, GPU LRU state, and fused attention-time resolution.

Host blocks use the same token hashes as their resident counterparts, but their hashes are published only after the contents are durable. Spilling therefore preserves prefix-cache value without allowing an incomplete host write to be reused.
P/D and NIXL integration
NIXL remains the P/D transport; HiSparse determines the decoder-side landing policy. The decoder chooses one policy per request during admission:

If the imported prefix fits in the normal GPU pools, NIXL writes it into resident device pages.
Otherwise, the bulk sparse-MLA KV lands in the registered HiSparse host pool. Device-only regions such as the indexer are still imported to GPU, the request receives its fixed hot-buffer allocation, and pages needed immediately are mirrored into resident GPU pages.

The two generic connector prerequisites below are intentionally separate from HiSparse:

#53779 lets connectors select externally transferable cache groups while retaining their scheduler group IDs.
#53780 carries stride, capacity, block size, group mapping, and identity per NIXL region, allowing P/D peers with different layouts and memory placement.

#53263 is a separate, optional optimization for same-node P/D. It stages device-to-host NIXL reads through decoder GPU memory to avoid UCX’s slow TCP loopback path. It is not required by the intended multi-node P/D design.
Scope
This PR implements the NVIDIA sparse-MLA path and includes the staging required for correct local or mixed prefill on a decode worker. Metrics are split into #53782, and DeepSeek V4’s compressed cache geometry is split into #53592.
